passages.text: Resveratrol and curcumin stimulate the expression of anti-apoptotic and inhibit pro-apoptotic gene products in chondrocytes

It is known that NF-kappaB regulates the expression of the anti-apoptotic proteins Bcl-2, Bcl-xL and TRAF1. To evaluate whether resveratrol and curcumin can modulate the expression of these anti-apoptotic genes products, we examined IL-1beta-stimulated primary human chondrocytes with or without pre-treatment of resveratrol and curcumin by western blot analysis (Figure 5a). IL-1beta inhibited the expression of Bcl-2, Bcl-xL and TRAF1 in a time-dependent manner. In contrast to this, the combinational treatment of resveratrol and curcumin stimulated the expression of the above-mentioned anti-apoptotic proteins in the same manner in chondrocytes (Figure 5a).

Effects of resveratrol and curcumin on IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB-dependent gene products in primary chondrocytes. (a) The effect of resveratrol/curcumin on IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB-dependent anti-apoptotic gene products in primary chondrocytes was studied. To determine whether resveratrol and curcumin treatment actively stimulates the production of anti-apoptotic gene products, primary chondrocyte cultures were either stimulated for 0, 12, 24, and 48 hours with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta or pre-treated with resveratrol and curcumin (50/50 muM) followed by 0, 12, 24, and 48 hours stimulation with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta. Equal amounts (500 ng protein per lane) of total proteins were separated by 10% SDS-PAGE and analysed by immunoblotting with anti-Bcl-2, anti-Bcl-xL and anti-TNF-alpha receptor-associated factor 1 (anti-TRAF1) antibodies. A time-dependent downregulation of the expression of Bcl-2, Bcl-xL and TRAF1 by IL-1beta was observed. In contrast, pre-treatment with resveratrol and curcumin resulted in a time-dependent increase of these anti-apoptotic proteins. Synthesis of the housekeeping protein beta-actin remained unaffected. (b) The effect of resveratrol/curcumin on IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB-dependent pro-apoptotic protein caspase-3 was also studied in primary chondrocytes. Whole cell lysates of primary chondrocyte cultures were either stimulated for 0, 12, 24, and 48 hours with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta or pre-treated with resveratrol and curcumin (50/50 muM) followed by 0, 12, 24, and 48 hours of stimulation with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta-, and evaluated with western blot analysis to examine the effect on the pro-apoptotic protein caspase-3. Equal amounts (500 ng protein per lane) of total proteins were separated by 12% SDS-PAGE and analysed by immunoblotting with an antibody against active caspase-3. Stimulation of the cultures with IL-1beta resulted in a time-dependent activation of caspase-3. In contrast, combinational treatment of resveratrol and curcumin inhibited caspase-3 activation in a time-dependent manner. Synthesis of the housekeeping protein beta-actin was not affected.

Furthermore, we wanted to know whether resveratrol and curcumin also suppress the IL-1beta-induced pro-apoptotic gene product, activated caspase-3, in the same cell cultures. To determine this, primary human chondrocytes were incubated with IL-1beta (10 ng/ml) alone for the indicated time or were pre-incubated with resveratrol and curcumin (50/50 muM) for 4 hours and then co-treated with IL-1beta (10 ng/ml) for the indicated time. As shown in Figure 5b, pre-treatment with resveratrol and curcumin significantly downregulated the level of biologically active caspase-3 in IL-1beta-stimulated cultures compared with primary human chondrocytes stimulated with IL-1beta alone.
Resveratrol and curcumin inhibit IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB-dependent proinflammatory and matrix degradation gene products in chondrocytes

We investigated whether resveratrol and curcumin can modulate IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB-regulated gene products involved in the inflammation and degradation processes in cartilage tissue. It has been shown previously in chondrocytes that IL-1beta stimulation activates Cox-2, VEGF, MMP-3 and MMP-9 expression. We therefore investigated whether both natural products are able to inhibit the IL-1beta-induced expression of these proteins. Primary human chondrocytes with or without pre-treatment with resveratrol and curcumin were examined for IL-1beta-induced gene products by western blot analysis using specific antibodies (Figure 6). IL-1beta induced the expression of Cox-2, MMP-3, MMP-9 and VEGF in a time-dependent manner, and the combinational treatment of resveratrol and curcumin inhibited the expression of the above-mentioned proteins in primary chondrocytes (Figure 6). Synthesis of the housekeeping protein beta-actin remained unaffected (Figure 6).

Effects of resveratrol and curcumin on IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB-dependent proinflammatory and matrix-degrading gene products in primary chondrocytes. To evaluate whether resveratrol and curcumin exert time-dependent effects on IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB-dependent expression of proinflammatory and matrix-degrading gene products, primary chondrocyte cultures were either stimulated for 0, 12, 24, and 48 hours with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta or pre-treated with resveratrol and curcumin (50 muM each) followed by 0, 12, 24, and 48 hours of stimulation with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta; after extraction of whole cell lysates (500 ng protein per lane), they were probed for the expression of matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-3, MMP-9, cylcooxygenase-2 (Cox-2) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) by western blot analysis. Stimulation of IL-1beta alone consistently resulted in time-dependent production of MMP-3, MMP-9, Cox-2 and VEGF. In contrast, pre-treatment with resveratrol and curcumin downregulated MMP-3, MMP-9, Cox-2 and VEGF time dependently. Synthesis of the housekeeping protein beta-actin was unaffected.
Effect of resveratrol and/or curcumin on IL-1beta-induced inhibition of collagen type II production in chondrocytes

Serum-starved human articular chondrocytes were cultured for 24 hours and then treated with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta, 50 muM resveratrol, 50 muM curcumin, and with 50 muM resveratrol and 50 muM curcumin, or were pre-treated with 50 muM resveratrol, 50 muM curcumin, and 50 muM resveratrol and 50 muM curcumin for 4 hours and then co-treated with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta, or left untreated and evaluated after 24 hours (Figure 7). Treatment of chondrocytes with 50 muM curcumin, with 50 muM resveratrol or with 50 muM resveratrol and 50 muM curcumin resulted in a stimulation of collagen type II production. Primary human chondrocytes stimulated with IL-1beta alone showed a significant downregulation of synthesis of collagen type II. In contrast, pre-treatment of chondrocytes with the phytochemical agents followed by stimulation with IL-1beta resulted in an inhibition of cytokine-induced effects on collagen type II production (Figure 7a, panel I). Interestingly, co-treatment of the chondrocytes with combinations of the two phytochemical agents increased the levels of these proteins more than each agent by itself.

Effects of resveratrol and curcumin on IL-1beta-induced inhibition of collagen type II and Sox-9 production in chondrocytes. To evaluate the effects of resveratrol and curcumin on IL-1beta-stimulated chondrogenic inhibition in primary chondrocytes, whole cell lysates (500 ng protein per lane) were probed with antibodies to (a) collagen type II (panel I), as the most abundant cartilage-specific extracellular matrix protein, and (b) the chondrogenic-specific transcription factor Sox-9 (panel I). Cultures were treated with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta, 50 muM resveratrol, 50 muM curcumin, 50 muM resveratrol and 50 muM curcumin, or were pre-treated with 50 muM resveratrol, 50 muM curcumin, 50 muM resveratrol and 50 muM curcumin for 4 hours and then co-treated with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta, or left untreated for 24 hours. Untreated cultures had strong (a) collagen type II and (b) Sox-9 and stimulation with IL-1beta alone greatly reduced collagen type II as well as Sox-9 production. However, pre-treatment of the cultures with resveratrol, curcumin or a combination of both inhibited the adverse effects of IL-1beta and the chondrocytes produced large quantities of collagen type II and Sox-9 at levels similar to control cultures. This was confirmed by quantitative densitometry (a, panel II and b, panel II). The mean values and standard deviations from three independent experiments are shown. White, grey and solid bars represent different molecular forms of collagen type II. Synthesis of the housekeeping protein beta-actin remained unaffected.
Effect of resveratrol and/or curcumin on Sox-9 in the chondrocyte nucleus

Sox-9 is a master specific transcription factor that controls the expression of chondrocyte-specific ECM protein genes and plays a pivotal role in chondrocyte differentiation. To test the hypothesis that phytochemicals are able to activate the transcription factor Sox-9 in human chondrocytes, monolayer cultures of human chondrocytes were either left unstimulated or stimulated with resveratrol and/or curcumin or were pre-treated with resveratrol and/or curcumin (50/50 muM) for 4 hours and then stimulated with IL-1beta for 24 hours, and the cell lysates were analysed by immunoblotting.

The results demonstrated that resveratrol and/or curcumin stimulated Sox-9 expression and inhibited the IL-1beta-induced decreased Sox-9 expression (Figure 7b, panel I). Because these data indicate that both phytochemicals have similar properties, we further investigated the cumulative role of resveratrol (50 muM) and curcumin (50 muM) on IL-1beta-induced inhibition of Sox-9 expression in chondrocytes. The results suggest that signalling from exposure to extracellular resveratrol and curcumin converge to influence the activity of transcription factors such as Sox-9, which are necessary for the expression of cartilage matrix genes (Figure 7b). Quantitative analysis (Figure 7a, panel II and 7b, panel II) of the western blot results confirmed that resveratrol and/or curcumin increase the expression of collagen type II (Figure 7a, panel II) and Sox-9 (Figure 7b, panel II) and inhibit the IL-1beta-induced decrease in collagen type II and Sox-9 expression. Data shown are representative of three independent experiments.
Resveratrol and curcumin block IL-1beta-induced nuclear translocation of NF-kappaB as revealed by APAAP

NF-kappaB is an important transcriptional regulator of inflammatory cytokines gene expression and plays a crucial role in inflammatory responses. After phosphorylation, ubiquitination and degradation of IkappaBalpha, the NF-kappaB fragment is translocated to the nucleus where it binds and activates the promoter of target genes. This translocation of NF-kappaB to the nucleus is necessary for regulation of gene expression by NF-kappaB.

Primary human chondrocytes were either left untreated (Figure 8a, A), or treated with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta alone for 5, 15 and 30 minutes (Figure 8a, panels B-D), or pre-treated with resveratrol and/or curcumin (50/50 muM) for 4 hours and then stimulated with IL-1beta for the same time periods (Figure 8a, panels E-G). In untreated control cultures, only cytoplasmic labelling of NF-kappaB was observed (Figure 8a, panel A). After 15 minutes of treatment, IL-1beta-stimulated chondrocytes showed a clear and positive labelling for activated NF-kappaB in the nuclei and to a lesser extent in the cytoplasm of chondrocytes (Figure 8a, panels B-D). Chondrocytes that were pre-treated with resveratrol and curcumin 50/50 muM (4 hours) and then co-treated with IL-1beta and resveratrol and curcumin showed positive staining in the cytoplasm and showed a clearly decreased, nuclear NF-kappaB staining (Figure 8a, panels E-G).

Inhibition of IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB activation and nuclear translocation by resveratrol and curcumin in primary chondrocytes using APAAP. (a) Human chondrocyte cultures either served as controls (panel A, not treated) or treated either with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta 5, 15 and 30 minutes alone or pre-treated with 50 muM resveratrol and 50 muM curcumin for 4 hours and then co-treated with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta for 5, 15 and 30 minutes, before immunolabelling with phospho-p65 antibodies. In control cells, anti-phospho-p65 labelling was restricted to the cytoplasm (panel A). Cells treated with IL-1beta alone revealed nuclear translocation of phospho-p65 (panels B-D) that was inhibited by co-treatment with resveratrol and curcumin (panels E-G). Data shown are representative of three independent experiments. A-G: x 160, bar = 50 mum. (b) Panel I: western blot analysis with IL-1beta-treated chondrocyte nuclear extracts. Serum-starved chondrocytes were pre-incubated with 50 muM resveratrol and 50 muM curcumin for 5, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 minutes, co-treated with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta for 30 minutes, and then probed for phospho-p65 by western blot analysis using antibodies to phospho-specific p65 and poly(ADP-Ribose) polymerase (PARP) (control). Resveratrol and curcumin pre-treatment inhibited IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB activation in a time-dependent manner. NF-kappaB nuclear translocation was inhibited completely after 50 minutes of pre-treatment with resveratrol and curcumin. Panel II: serum-starved human chondrocytes were pre-incubated with resveratrol and curcumin at various concentrations (5 muM, 10 muM, 20 muM, 30 muM, 40 muM and 50 muM each) for 4 hours followed by 10 ng/ml IL-1beta stimulation for 30 minutes. The nuclear extracts (500 ng protein per lane) were probed for phospho-p65 by western blot analysis using antibodies to phospho-specific p65 and PARP (control). A concentration-dependent inhibition of NF-kappaB nuclear translocation was observed. At a concentration of 40 muM resveratrol and 40 muM curcumin, NF-kappaB nuclear translocation was completely inhibited. The inhibition of NF-kappaB nuclear translocation by resveratrol and curcumin is therefore concentration as well as time dependent. Synthesis of PARP remained unaffected in nuclear extracts.
Resveratrol and curcumin inhibit NF-kappaB activation caused by IL-1beta in a concentration-dependent and time-dependent manner in chondrocytes

To examine whether resveratrol and curcumin block the IL-1beta-induced activation of NF-kappaB, nuclear protein extracts from serum-starved chondrocytes were probed for the phosphorylated form of the p65 NF-kappaB subunit after pre-treatment with 50 muM resveratrol and 50 muM curcumin for the indicated times followed by 10 ng/ml IL-1beta stimulation for 30 minutes (Figure 8b, panel I). Furthermore, chondrocytes were pre-incubated with the indicated concentrations of resveratrol and curcumin for 4 hours followed by co-treatment with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta and resveratrol and curcumin for 30 minutes (Figure 8b, panel II). The western blot results confirmed that co-treatment of resveratrol and curcumin had no effect on NF-kappaB activation. Resveratrol and curcumin, however, inhibited IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB activation in a time-dependent (Figure 8b, panel I) and a concentration-dependent (Figure 8b, panel II) manner.
Resveratrol but not curcumin inhibits IL-1beta-induced IkappaBalpha degradation

Resveratrol and curcumin inhibited IL-1beta-induced activation of NF-kappaB and its translocation to the chondrocyte nucleus. We therefore examined the upstream mechanisms of NF-kappaB activation by IL-1beta in chondrocytes. It is well known that an important pre-requisite for the activation of NF-kappaB is the phosphorylation and degradation of IkappaBalpha, the natural blocker of NF-kappaB.

To test whether inhibition of IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB activation occurs through inhibition of IkappaBalpha degradation or through inhibition of IKK activation, we treated chondrocyte cultures for 8 hours with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta alone or with 100 muM of the specific proteasome inhibitor ALLN, which prevents the degradation of phosphorylated IkappaBalpha by the 26S proteasome. Other serum-starved human articular chondrocytes were pre-stimulated with 50 muM resveratrol, 50 muM curcumin or 100 muM ALLN alone for 4 hours and then co-treated with IL-1beta (10 ng/ml) for 8 hours. Additionally, other serum-starved human articular chondrocytes were pre-stimulated with 50 muM resveratrol or 50 muM curcumin alone for 4 hours and then co-treated with IL-1beta (10 ng/ml) for 8 hours. Some cultures were left untreated and evaluated after 12 hours. The activation of pIkappaBalpha in the cytoplasm of the chondrocytes was determined by western blot analysis using anti-IkappaBalpha and anti-beta-actin (control) antibodies. IL-1beta induced IkappaBalpha degradation in untreated cultures, but IL-1beta could not induce IkappaBalpha degradation in resveratrol pre-treated chondrocytes - in contrast to curcumin pre-treated cells (Figure 9). Taken together, these results suggest that in contrast to curcumin resveratrol blocks IL-1beta-induced IkappaBalpha degradation. Data shown are representative of three independent experiments.

Effects of resveratrol and curcumin treatment on IL-1beta-induced IkappaBalpha degradation. Serum-starved human chondrocytes were pre-treated with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta alone for 4 hours, or with 100 muM N-Ac-Leu-Leu-norleucinal (ALLN) for 30 minutes, or pre-treated with 50 muM resveratrol, 50 muM curcumin or 100 muM ALLN alone for 4 hours and then co-treated with IL-1beta (10 ng/ml) for 8 hours. Other serum-starved chondrocytes were pre-treated with 50 muM resveratrol or 50 muM curcumin alone for 4 hours and then co-treated with IL-1beta (10 ng/ml) for 8 hours. Some cultures were left untreated and evaluated after 12 hours. Cytoplasmic extracts (500 ng protein per lane) were fractionated and then subjected to western blotting with phosphospecific IkappaBalpha antibody. The data demonstrate that resveratrol (but not curcumin) inhibits IL-1beta-induced IkappaBalpha degradation. Data shown are representative of three independent experiments. The same membrane was re-blotted with antibodies to beta-actin.
Resveratrol but not curcumin inhibits IL-1beta-dependent ubiquitination of IkappaBalpha

Next we determined whether resveratrol or curcumin affected the IL-1beta-induced IkappaBalpha ubiquitination that leads to IkappaBalpha degradation. We treated some chondrocyte cultures with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta alone or with 100 muM ALLN for 8 hours. Other serum-starved human articular chondrocytes were pre-stimulated with 50 muM resveratrol, 50 muM curcumin or 100 muM ALLN alone for 4 hours and then co-treated with IL-1beta (10 ng/ml) for 8 hours. Other serum-starved human articular chondrocytes were pre-stimulated with 50 muM resveratrol or 50 muM curcumin alone for 4 hours and then co-treated with IL-1beta (10 ng/ml) for 8 hours. Some cultures were left untreated and evaluated after 12 hours. Western blot analysis using an antibody that detects IkappaBalpha indicated that IL-1beta induced IkappaBalpha ubiquitination, as indicated by high molecular weight bands, and that mainly resveratrol, but not curcumin, suppressed this ubiquitination (Figure 10). Mainly resveratrol, but not curcumin, therefore inhibited IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB activation by inhibiting phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and degradation of IkappaBalpha (Figure 10). Data shown are representative of three independent experiments.

Effects of resveratrol and curcumin treatment on IL-1beta-induced IkappaBalpha ubiquitination. Serum-starved human chondrocytes were pre-treated with 10 ng/ml IL-1beta alone for 4 hours, or 100 muM N-Ac-Leu-Leu-norleucinal (ALLN) for 30 minutes, or pre-treated with 50 muM resveratrol, 50 muM curcumin or 100 muM ALLN alone for 4 hours and then co-treated with IL-1beta (10 ng/ml) for 8 hours. Other serum-starved chondrocytes were pre-treated with 50 muM resveratrol or 50 muM curcumin alone for 4 hours and then co-treated with IL-1beta (10 ng/ml) for 8 hours. Some cultures were left untreated and evaluated after 12 hours. Cytoplasmic extracts were immunoprecipitated with an antibody against IkappaBalpha and subjected to western blot analysis using a monoclonal anti-ubiquitin antibody. Resveratrol (but not curcumin), stabilized IL-1beta-induced ubiquitination of IkappaBalpha. Data shown are representative of three independent experiments.
Resveratrol does not inhibit IL-1beta-induced IKK activation

As we could demonstrate, resveratrol inhibits the degradation and ubiquitination of IkappaBalpha. We now further evaluated the effect of resveratrol on IL-1beta-induced IKK activation, which is required for IL-1beta-induced phosphorylation of IkappaBalpha. The results from the immune complex kinase assay showed that IL-1beta activated IKK as early as 5 minutes after IL-1beta treatment, but that resveratrol did not inhibit IL-1beta-induced activation of IKK (Figure 11a, panel I). IL-1beta or resveratrol had no direct effect on the expression of IKK protein (Figure 11a, panels II and III).

Effects of resveratrol and curcumin treatment on IL-1beta-induced IkappaB kinase activation. Serum-starved primary human chondrocytes were pre-treated with (a) 50 muM resveratrol or (b) 50 muM curcumin for 4 hours and then co-treated with IL-1beta (10 ng/ml) for the indicated times. Whole cell extracts were immunoprecipitated with an antibody against IkappaB kinase (IKK)-alpha and analysed by an immune complex kinase assay. To examine the effect of curcumin on the expression level of IKK proteins, whole cell extracts (500 ng protein per lane) were fractionated by SDS-PAGE and examined using western blot analysis with anti-IKK-alpha and anti-IKK-beta antibodies. Data shown are representative of three independent experiments. The results demonstrate that resveratrol does not affect IL-1beta-induced IKK activation.
Curcumin but not resveratrol inhibits IL-1beta-induced IkappaBalpha kinase activation

Since we could demonstrate that curcumin inhibits the phosphorylation of IkappaBalpha, we then evaluated whether curcumin has an effect on IL-1beta-induced IKK activation, which is required for IL-1beta-induced phosphorylation of IkappaBalpha. Curcumin completely suppressed IL-1beta-induced activation of IKK (Figure 11b, panel I). IL-1beta or curcumin had no direct effect on the expression of IKK protein (Figure 11b, panels II and III).
Discussion

The aim of the present study was to determine if the anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects of resveratrol and curcumin in primary human chondrocytes are mediated by similar signalling mechanisms and whether combining these natural compounds has a synergistic effect on IL-1beta-mediated cellular responses, NF-kappaB-mediated signal transduction pathways and regulation of NF-kappaB-regulated gene expression.

The study leads to the following findings: IL-1beta-induced suppression of chondrocytes viability and proliferation is revoked by resveratrol and curcumin pre-treatment. Stimulation of chondrocytes with IL-1beta results in morphological alterations (that is, swollen mitochondria, dilated endoplasmic reticulum and apoptosis) that were abolished through pre-treatment with resveratrol and curcumin. Co-treatment of the IL-1beta-stimulated cells with both resveratrol and/or curcumin inhibits activation of PARP cleavage. Resveratrol potentiates the anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects of curcumin on IL-1beta-stimulated chondrocytes, and this correlates with downregulation of NF-kappaB-specific gene products that are known to mediate inflammation, degradation and apoptosis of chondrocytes in OA. Additionally, both resveratrol and/or curcumin suppressed IL-1beta-induced downregulation of the cartilage-specific ECM component collagen type II and of the cartilage-specific master transcription factor Sox-9. The activation and translocation of p65 from the cytoplasm to the nucleus could be inhibited clearly by resveratrol and curcumin in IL-1beta-stimulated human chondrocytes. Both resveratrol and curcumin inhibited NF-kappaB activation in a concentration-dependent and time-dependent manner. Finally, inhibition of NF-kappaB activation by resveratrol occurred mainly through the accumulation of phosphorylated IkappaBalpha, ubiquitinated IkappaBalpha and inhibition of proteasome activity - in contrast to this, in the case of curcumin it was mainly caused through inhibition of IKK activation.

Proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha and IL-1beta have been shown to mediate cartilage degradation and apoptosis in chondrocytes in degenerative joint diseases such as RA and OA in humans as well as in animals. Indeed, cytokine-mediated apoptosis of chondrocytes is believed to play a key role in the pathogenesis of OA. These proinflammatory cytokines are produced by activated synoviocytes, macrophages and chondrocytes. They are well known to activate the ubiquitous transcription factor NF-kappaB, which leads to further production and upregulation of proinflammatory cytokines and enzymes such as Cox-2 and MMPs, which in turn produce prostaglandins and degrade ECM macromolecules leading to cartilage degradation and further joint inflammation. Although numerous effects have been described for resveratrol and curcumin, however, the mechanisms responsible for their anti-inflammatory effects in chondrocytes are not yet clear.

Activation of NF-kappaB provides the potential link between inflammation and hyperplasia during OA and RA in the joint. The use of a specific NF-kappaB inhibitor has been reported to result in a significant decrease in joint swelling in mice with collagen-induced arthritis. NF-kappaB therefore represents an important target for therapeutic strategies aimed at the prophylactic treatment of inflammatory disorders, such as OA and RA.

Resveratrol and curcumin are anti-inflammatory dietary phytochemicals that have previously been shown to antagonize some catabolic effects of TNFalpha and IL-1beta via inhibition of NF-kappaB in different cell types. We have previously demonstrated that in chondrocytes resveratrol inhibits NF-kappaB through suppression of the proteasome activity, and this leads to the accumulation of phosphorylated IkappaBalpha and inhibition of p65. Curcumin has been shown to inhibit NF-kappaB activation in chondrocytes and other cell lines of various origins. However, whether curcumin can also inhibit NF-kappaB activation through inhibition of the proteasome activity or IKK activation in chondrocytes has not been previously reported.

We found that inhibition of IKK by curcumin, which is needed for NF-kappaB activation, led to inhibition of phosphorylation of both IkappaBalpha and p65 but the proteasome was not affected by curcumin. We also found that resveratrol and curcumin in combination stimulated several genes that are regulated by NF-kappaB, including anti-apoptotic gene products (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL and TRAF1). Resveratrol and curcumin inhibited pro-apoptotic proteins (caspase-3, PARP) and matrix degrading gene products (MMP3 and MMP-9), and angiogenesis and inflammation gene products (VEGF and Cox-2). It has been reported that the expression of Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL is known to be regulated by NF-kappaB and can block cell death induced by a variety of agents. In the present study we could indeed demonstrate the synergistic effects of naturally occurring polyphenolic compounds resveratrol and curcumin on NF-kappaB activation and the regulation of expression of its target gene products.

It is not clear whether these effects of resveratrol and curcumin are mediated only by targeting NF-kappaB; on the contrary, it is absolutely possible that resveratrol and curcumin mediate their effects by targeting more than one cell signalling pathway. However, if this was the case, then the beneficial effects that resveratrol and curcumin might have in OA and RA therapy would be further emphasized, as recent reports have demonstrated that multi-targeted therapy has a better chance of success against inflammation and cancer compared with therapies that aim for a single target.

It is well known that the cartilage-specific transcription factor Sox-9 is required for expression of cartilage-specific ECM genes. We also observed a reduction in collagen type II and Sox-9 expression in chondrocytes after treatment with IL-1beta, consistent with previous reports of articular chondrocytes from our and other laboratories. We further observed, however, an inhibition of IL-1beta-induced downregulation of collagen type II and Sox-9 expression by pre-treating the cells with resveratrol or curcumin. Moreover, we extended these studies by pre-treating the cells with a combination of resveratrol and curcumin, revealing further inhibition of IL-1beta-induced reduction in collagen type II and Sox-9 expression compared with each compound alone. These changes in expression of collagen type II and Sox-9 in response to resveratrol and curcumin are probably due to alternate modes of regulation, independent of changes in NF-kappaB. Consistent with these findings, previous studies from other laboratories have shown that cytokines partially reduce Sox-9 protein levels over a period of 8 hours through a NF-kappaB-dependent, post-transcriptional mechanism in mouse chondrocytes - demonstrating how active transcription factors, sharing common co-factors, regulate gene expression.
Conclusions

The results presented here suggest that the anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects of resveratrol and/or curcumin are mediated through crosstalk among the inhibition of the IKK-induced and proteasome-induced NF-kappaB pathway, which are activated by a wide variety of proinflammatory agents. Based on these results, we conclude that both resveratrol and curcumin are direct inhibitors of IKK and the proteasome; through this inhibition they block NF-kappaB and NF-kappaB-regulated gene expression (Figure 12). However, since a large variety of intracellular signalling pathways interact and converge in chondrocytes, we do not exclude that both resveratrol and curcumin may have additional molecular targets in these cells. Consequently they may also influence inflammatory and apoptotic pathways using other mechanisms.

Inhibitory effects of resveratrol and curcumin on IL-1beta-induced NF-kappaB activation and apoptosis in primary human chondrocytes in vitro. IL-1beta stimulates the IL-1beta receptor, intiating an intracellular signal transduction cascade, which activates the cytoplasmic IkappaBalpha kinases (IKK)-alpha, IKK-beta, and IKK-gamma. These kinases phosphoryle inactive IkappaBalpha. Phosphorylated IkappaBalpha is then ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome and active NF-kappaB is released. NF-kappaB translocates to the nucleus, where it activates proinflammatory and pro-apoptotic gene production. In chondrocytes, resveratrol and curcumin both inhibit the NF-kappaB signal transduction pathway but in different ways: resveratrol inhibits ubiquitination of phosphorylated IkappaBalpha, and blocks translocation of the activated NF-kappaB to the nucleus. In a similar fashion to resveratrol, curcumin also inhibits translocation of the activated NF-kappaB to the nucleus. However in contrast to resveratrol, curcumin does not have a degradation inhibiting effect on phosphorylated IkappaBalpha. Instead, curcumin inhibits IL-1beta signalling at an earlier point by inhibition of IKK-alpha, IKK-beta, and IKK-gamma.

Further in vitro and in vivo studies in animals and humans will be required to determine the full potential of the synergistic effects of both resveratrol and curcumin and their potential for the prevention and treatment of OA and RA.

passages.text: Differential Response to Trichloroethylene-Induced Hepatosteatosis in Wild-Type and PPARalpha-Humanized Mice
Background

Trichloroacetic acid, an oxidative metabolite of trichloroethylene (TRI), is a ligand of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR) alpha, which is involved in lipid homeostasis and anti-inflammation.
Objective
We examined the role of mouse and human PPARalpha in TRI-induced hepatic steatosis and toxicity.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Methods

Male wild-type (mPPARalpha), Pparalpha-null, and humanized PPARalpha (hPPARalpha) mice on an Sv/129 background were exposed via inhalation to 0, 1,000, and 2,000 ppm TRI for 8 hr/day for 7 days. We assessed TRI-induced steatosis or hepatic damage through biochemical and histopathological measurements.

infons.name: Chemical and Drug Induced Liver Injury

passages.text: Results

Plasma alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase activities increased in all mouse lines after exposure to 1,000 and 2,000 ppm TRI. Exposure induced hepatocyte necrosis and inflammatory cells in all mouse lines, but hepatic lipid accumulation was observed only in Pparalpha-null and hPPARalpha mice. No differences were observed in TRI-mediated induction of hepatic PPARalpha target genes except for a few genes that differed between mPPARalpha and hPPARalpha mice. However, TRI significantly increased expression of triglyceride (TG)-synthesizing enzymes, diacylglicerol acyltransferases, and PPARgamma in Pparalpha-null and hPPARalpha mice, which may account for the increased TG in their livers. TRI exposure elevated nuclear factor-kappa B (NFkappaB) p52 mRNA and protein in all mice regardless of PPARalpha genotype.
Conclusions

NFkappaB-p52 is a candidate molecular marker for inflammation caused by TRI, and PPARalpha may be involved in TRI-induced hepatosteatosis. However, human PPARalpha may afford only weak protection against TRI-mediated effects compared with mouse PPARalpha.

Trichloroethylene (TRI) is a chlorinated solvent that has been used as a degreaser and as an intermediate in synthesizing other chemicals. Occupational TRI exposure is declining in industrialized countries because of technological innovation and legislation, but it is increasing in emerging industrialized countries, especially in Asia. TRI exposure has been associated with rat renal and mouse liver injury, impaired reproductive function in male mice, autoimmune hepatitis in the autoimmune-prone MRL mouse model, and allergic hepatitis in the guinea pig maximization test. Recently, occupational exposure to TRI was associated with severe hypersensitive skin damage and impaired hepatic function.

infons.name: Chemical and Drug Induced Liver Injury

passages.text: TRI is metabolized through oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP) isozymes such as CYP1A1/2, CYP2B1/2, CYP2C11, and CYP2E1. CYP2E1 is the most important enzyme in the conversion of TRI to chloral hydrate through intermediate metabolite(s) formation, which is rapidly metabolized to trichloroacetic acid (TCA) by aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) or to trichloroethanol (TCE) by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH). TCE can be converted to TCA by ADH and ALDH via chloral hydrate. In addition, a small portion of TRI is conjugated by glutathione S-transferase (GST) to form S-(dichlorovinyl) glutathione and further metabolized to S-(1,2-dichlorovinyl)-l cysteine, which is considered a kidney carcinogen. An intermediate metabolite(s) of TRI to chloral hydrate is thought to induce hepatic damage.

passages.text: Peroxisome proliferators function as ligands for the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARalpha), a nuclear receptor that regulates genes involved in fatty acid transport and beta-oxidation, resulting in increased fatty acid catabolism and increases in the number and size of peroxisomes in the livers of exposed mice or rats. TCA and DCA both activate PPARalpha in the liver, but other TRI metabolites do not. also reported the activation of PPARalpha by TRI, TCA, or DCA treatment in PPARalpha wild-type mice, judging from the induction of PPARalpha-related gene expressions, but not in Pparalpha-null mice. In addition, reported that PPARalpha was activated after TRI exposure in wild-type but not CYP2E1-null mice, which they attributed to a lack of CYP2E1-mediated production of TCA.

Whether activation of PPARalpha is involved in TRI-induced liver injury remains to be clarified. PPARalpha activation is accompanied by increased hepatic lipid turnover via the beta-oxidation system, which reduces lipid accumulation that can result in hepatic toxicity. PPARalpha activation also can inhibit proinflammatory nuclear factor-kappa B (NFkappaB) by interacting with the p65 and p50 heterodimer, and anti-inflammatory effects via PPARalpha-mediated inhibition of NFkappaB DNA binding activity have been demonstrated in human hepatocytes. However, although the consequences of PPARalpha activation in the mouse liver is relatively well defined, the consequences of human PPARalpha activation in response to TRI and other peroxisome proliferators is still poorly understood.

passages.text: Another PPAR subtype, PPARgamma, regulates genes involved in adipogenesis and lipid metabolism. PPARgamma may also be involved in TRI-induced hepatosteatosis, as TCA also activates mouse PPARgamma, and guinea pigs suffering from TRI-induced toxic liver injury showed fatty changes of the liver. In the present study, we investigated TRI-induced subacute hepatotoxicity in mPPARalpha, Pparalpha-null and humanized PPARalpha (hPPARalpha) mice to clarify differences in the roles of human and mouse PPARalpha in TRI toxicity.

Chemical and Drug Induced Liver Injury

passages.text: Materials and Methods
Chemicals

TRI was provided by the Japan Association for Hygiene of Chlorinated Solvents, and its purity was determined to be at least 99% as judged by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). All other chemicals were purchased from commercial sources and were of the highest purity available.
Animals

This study was conducted according to the Animal Experimental Guidelines of the Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine. Male wild-type (mPPARalpha), Pparalpha-null, and hPPARalphaTet-OFF (hPPARalpha) mice on an Sv/129 genetic background were bred as described elsewhere and reared at the Institute of Laboratory Animal Research (Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine). The expression of human PPARalpha cDNA in hPPARalphaTet-OFF mice is limited to hepatocytes and is under the control of the tetracycline regulatory system, as described by. All mice were housed in a room under a 12:12 hr light:dark cycle (lights on at 0900 hours and off at 2100 hours), with stable relative humidity (57-60%) and a constant temperature (23-25 C). Food and water were provided ad libitum, and all animals were treated humanely and with regard for the alleviation of suffering. When the mice were 10 weeks of age, each strain was randomly divided into three groups of six animals each.
TRI exposure

Each group of mice was exposed to 0, 1,000, or 2,000 ppm TRI [equivalent to 0, 800, and 1,600 mg/kg/day by gavage, respectively ] or fresh air in an inhalation chamber for 8 hr/day over 7 consecutive days, as described previously. In PPARalpha wild-type mice, TRI metabolism was previously shown to be saturated with exposure to approximately 1,000 ppm, but we evaluated exposure to 1,000 and 2,000 ppm because of limited information concerning TRI metabolism in Pparalpha-null and hPPARalpha mice. We studied exposure by inhalation, because this is the most common route of occupational exposure in humans. Occupational exposures are generally much lower than exposures used in this research but may approach these levels in some cases, for example, during defatting processes using immersion tanks. Mice were moved to individual metal metabolism cages to collect urine samples after 7 days, and were sacrificed by exsanguination through the abdominal aorta under pentobarbital anesthesia the following day. Plasma was separated from whole blood by centrifugation at 3,000 rpm for 10 min. The liver was carefully dissected out and immediately weighed, and a small section was excised from the median lobe of each mouse and fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin.
Plasma aminotransferase activities
We measured aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) activities by the colorimetric method using a Transaminase C II Test Kit (Wako, Osaka, Japan).
Triglyceride concentration
Lipid was extracted from livers using the method of, and hepatic and plasma triglyceride (TG) were measured by the colorimetric method using TG-IE kits (Wako).
Urinary metabolites

We measured urinary TCA and TCE concentrations by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) (6890N gas chromatograph, 5975 Mass Selective Detector, 7683 Automatic Liquid Sampler; Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA), as described previously.
Histopathology evaluation

Tissue blocks were embedded in paraffin and 5-mum sections were mounted on glass slides and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Photomicrographic images were captured on a BZ-8000 fluorescence microscope microscope (Keyence, Osaka, Japan). We identified steatosis based on the presence of vacuoles consistent with lipid accumulation; steatosis was classified as macrovesicular steatosis if the nucleus was displaced by the vacuole or as microvesicular steatosis if the nucleus remained in the center of the hepatocyte. Hepatocyte proliferation was classified based on the presence of enlarged hepatocytes with prominent eosinophilic cytoplasm. Cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and pycnotic or karyolitic nuclei were designated as necrotic.

Histopathological findings in 20 randomly selected 200x microscopic fields per section were scored for steatosis [0, none; 1, mild (5-33% of parenchymal involvement of steatosis); 2, moderate (33-66%); or 3, severe (> 66%)]; necrotic cells [0, no necrosis; 1, minimal (only occasional necrotic cells in any lobule); 2, mild (less than one-third of the lobular structure affected); 3, moderate (one-third to two-thirds of lobular structure affected); or 4, severe (greater than two-thirds of the lobular structure affected)]; lobular and portal tract inflammation [0, none; 1, mild (< 2 foci/field); 2, moderate (2-4 foci/field); or 3, severe (> 4 foci/field)]; and hepatocyte proliferation (0, absent; 1, present).
Real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
We isolated total RNA from whole liver using the RNeasy Mini Kit (QIAGEN, Tokyo, Japan). Real-time PCR analysis was performed as described elsewhere.
Western blot analysis

A section of liver from each mouse was homogenized with three volumes of 10 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) containing 0.25 M sucrose. The nuclear fraction (derived from both hepatocytes and nonparenchymal cells) was extracted using a CelLytic NuCLEAR Extraction Kit (Sigma, Tokyo, Japan). Nuclear fractions (NFkappaB-p65, NFkappaB-p50, NFkappaB-p52, and PPARalpha) and liver homogenates (other proteins include CYP2E1 and ALDH2) were subjected to 10% or 12.5% polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, as described elsewhere.
Statistical analysis

Data are expressed as mean +- SD. We used the Tukey-Kramer HSD test to compare genotype effects (vs. wild-type controls) and exposure effects in each strain. TCA and TCE were below the detection limit in all control groups, and metabolism was saturated at 1,000 ppm. Therefore, we compared levels of TCA and TCE, respectively, in exposed mice (1,000 and 2,000 ppm combined) between genotype groups. Histopathologic scores were compared using a nonparametric method (Steel-Dwass method). The alpha level for statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.
Results
Liver and body weight

We found significant differences among control (unexposed) mice according to genotype (Table 1). Specifically, the mean body weight of hPPARalpha mice was 14% less and 8.5% less than mPPARalpha and Pparalpha-null mice, respectively, and the mean liver weight of hPPARalpha mice was 11% less than Pparalpha-null mice; the liver/body weight ratio of Pparalpha-null mice was 11% higher than in mPPARalpha mice. TRI at 1,000 and 2,000 ppm significantly increased liver weight in the three mouse lines, and the increases were almost the same: 38% and 49% in mPPARalpha mice; 20% and 37% in Pparalpha-null mice; and 28% and 32% in hPPARalpha mice, respectively. However, the increases were not significantly different between TRI doses within each strain. Liver/body weight ratios were also significantly increased with TRI exposure at 1,000 and 2,000 ppm relative to controls (38% and 43% in mPPARalpha; 24% and 36% in Pparalpha-null, and 27% and 39% in hPPARalpha mice, respectively), with a significant difference between 2,000 and 1,000 ppm exposures in Pparalpha-null mice.
Urinary metabolites

We observed no differences in the volume of urine samples collected according to genotype or exposure concentration (data not shown). TCA and TCE levels were below the detection limit in all control mice (Table 1). TCA and TCE were detectable in all TRI-exposed mice but were not significantly different between the two TRI exposures within strains. TCA concentrations were significantly lower and TCE concentrations tended to be higher in exposed Pparalpha-null mice relative to exposed mPPARalpha mice. Mean concentrations of total TRI metabolites (TCA plus TCE) in mPPARalpha, Pparalpha-null, and hPPARalpha mice were 79.1, 97.9, and 73.8 mmol, respectively, with no significant differences among the genotypes.
Biochemical changes

AST and ALT liver injury biomarkers varied < 10% among control mice in each strain (Table 1). Plasma ALT and AST levels were significantly increased in all exposed mice relative to controls (41-74% and 36-79% higher, respectively), and mean levels within each group were higher, although not significantly different, with exposure to 2,000 versus 1,000 ppm TRI.
TG in plasma and liver

In unexposed mice, we observed significantly higher plasma TG levels in hPPARalpha versus mPPARalpha mice (52%), and significantly higher liver TG levels in hPPARalpha mice versus mPPARalpha and Pparalpha-null mice (77% and 30%, respectively) and in Pparalpha-null versus mPPARalpha mice (36%) (Table 1). Relative to unexposed mice, liver TG levels were significantly higher in Pparalpha-null mice exposed to 2,000 ppm TRI (113%) and in hPPARalpha mice exposed to 1,000 (58%) and 2,000 ppm (87%) TRI. However, there were no significant differences in mean plasma or liver TG concentrations between 2,000-ppm and 1,000-ppm TRI mice within groups. Hepatic TG levels were significantly correlated with liver/body ratios of all mice used in this study (r = 0.54).
Histopathological analysis

We observed neither necrosis nor inflammatory cells in liver sections from unexposed mice [Table 2, Figure 1A-C; see also Supplemental Material, Table 1 (doi:10.1289/ehp.1001928)], which is consistent with lower AST and ALT levels in these mice (Table 1). However, small cytoplasmic vacuoles were present in sections from unexposed Pparalpha-null and hPPARalpha mice, similar to the reports by and, respectively, resulting in steatosis scores > 0.

Steatosis was absent in the livers of TRI-exposed and unexposed mPPARalpha mice, but it was significantly increased in exposed versus unexposed Pparalpha-null and hPPARalpha mice; steatosis was significantly higher in Pparalpha-null mice exposed to 2,000 versus 1,000 ppm TRI [Table 2, Figure 1D-F; see also Supplemental Material, Table 1 (doi:10.1289/ehp.1001928)]. Steatosis scores were significantly correlated with liver TG levels of all mice used in this study (r = 0.75). However, macrovesicular steatosis was more common in hPPARalpha mice than in Pparalpha-null mice. Necrosis scores were significantly higher in TRI-exposed mice relative to controls in all three genotypes and were significantly higher with 2,000 versus 1,000 ppm TRI exposure in mPPARalpha and hPPARalpha mice. Inflammation scores were significantly higher than in controls with exposure to 2,000 ppm TRI in all three groups and significantly higher with 2,000 versus 1,000 ppm TRI in mPPARalpha mice. Hepatocyte proliferation was significantly increased with 2,000 ppm TRI exposure in mPPARalpha mice, but there was little evidence of an association with exposure in hPPARalpha mice and no evidence of proliferation in Pparalpha-null mice.
Real-time quantitative PCR

The background expression of several genes differed significantly between strains in control mice (Table 3). Specifically, very long chain acyl-coenzyme A (CoA) dehydrogenase (VLCAD), medium chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD), peroxisomal bifunctional protein (hydratase + 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase) (PH), peroxisomal thiolase (PT), diacylglicerol acyltransferase 1 (DGAT1), and p52 mRNA levels were higher in hPPARalpha mice than in mPPARalpha and Pparalpha-null mice. mRNA levels for PPARalpha, proliferation cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), p50, and tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFalpha) were higher in hPPARalpha mice than in mPPARalpha mice, whereas PPARgamma mRNA was lower in hPPARalpha mice than in Pparalpha-null mice [Table 3; see also Supplemental Material, Figure 1 (doi:10.1289/ehp.1001928)]. VLCAD, PH, and PT mRNA levels were significantly lower in Pparalpha-null mice than in mPPARalpha mice, and p50, p52, PPARgamma, and TNFalpha mRNA levels were higher in Pparalpha-null mice than in mPPARalpha mice.

TRI exposure did not increase the expression of human PPARalpha mRNA in hPPARalpha mice, but 2,000 ppm TRI significantly increased mouse PPARalpha mRNA in mPPARalpha mice (Table 3). PCNA mRNA expression and mRNA expression of the PPARalpha target genes VLCAD, MCAD, PH, and PT were increased with TRI exposure relative to controls in mPPARalpha and hPPARalpha mice, with more pronounced induction of PH and PT mRNA in mPPARalpha mice. However, we observed no significant differences in the expression of these genes between mice exposed to 1,000 versus 2,000 ppm TRI.

Relative to unexposed controls, DGAT1 and DGAT2 mRNA significantly increased in hPPARalpha mice exposed to 2,000 ppm TRI and in Pparalpha-null mice exposed to 1,000 and 2,000 ppm TRI (Table 3). PPARgamma mRNA significantly increased in Pparalpha-null and hPPARalpha mice exposed to 1,000 and 2,000 ppm TRI. In contrast, DGAT1, DGAT2, and PPARgamma mRNA levels did not differ with TRI exposure in mPPARalpha mice.

NFkappaB-p65 mRNA expression was significantly increased with TRI exposure in Pparalpha-null and hPPARalpha mice but not in mPPARalpha mice (Table 3). NFkappaB-p50 mRNA expression was significantly increased with exposure in Pparalpha-null mice only, but NFkappaB-p52 and TNFalpha mRNA expression was significantly increased with exposure in all strains. NFkappaB-p52 mRNA levels were significantly correlated with plasma ALT levels of all mice used in this study (r = 0.54).
Protein expression

Protein expression differed among strains in control mice (Table 3). PPARalpha levels were 10.4 times higher in unexposed hPPARalpha mice than in mPPARalpha mice [see Supplemental Material, Figure 2 (doi:10.1289/ehp.1001928)]. VLCAD, PT, acyl-CoA oxidase (ACOX) A, and ACOX B proteins were significantly higher in unexposed hPPARalpha mice than in mPPARalpha and Pparalpha-null mice, MCAD was lower in unexposed hPPARalpha and in Pparalpha-null mice than in mPPARalpha mice, and NFkappaB-p65 was lower in hPPARalpha mice than in Pparalpha-null mice. VLCAD, MCAD, PH, PT, ACOX A, and ACOX B expression was slightly lower and p65 and p52 expression was slightly higher in unexposed Pparalpha-null versus mPPARalpha mice.

Relative to controls, TRI exposure (both doses) significantly increased PPARalpha target gene proteins VLCAD, PH, PT, ACOX A, and ACOX B in mPPARalpha and hPPARalpha mice, but TRI exposure did not induce PPARalpha protein expression. MCAD protein was significantly increased with TRI exposure in hPPARalpha mice only. PCNA protein was higher in TRI-exposed mice compared with controls in all strains. NFkappaB-p52 and TNFalpha proteins were also increased with TRI exposure in all strains, whereas NFkappaB-p50 and -p65 proteins were increased only in exposed Pparalpha-null mice. 4-Hydroxy-2-nonenal protein, a marker of oxidative stress, was increased in Pparalpha-null mice exposed to 1,000 ppm TRI and in mPPARalpha and hPPARalpha mice exposed to 2,000 ppm TRI.

Additionally, we measured hepatic protein expression of CYP2E1 and ALDH2 enzymes, as urine TCA levels were significantly lower in Pparalpha-null than in mPPARalpha mice. We did not observe significant differences in the expression of either enzyme among controls (data not shown). TRI exposure did not influence hepatic CYP2E1 expression, but it did decrease ALDH2 expression to a comparable extent in all mouse lines (data not shown).
Discussion

Pparalpha-null and hPPARalpha mice appeared to be more susceptible to TRI toxicity than wild-type mPPARalpha mice, which suggests that PPARalpha may help protect mice against TRI-induced hepatotoxicity, especially from lipid accumulation. In particular, we noted increased liver TG levels and steatosis with TRI exposure in Pparalpha-null and hPPARalpha mice, but not in mPPARalpha mice. In contrast, PPARalpha did not appear to influence plasma AST or ALT concentration or the severity of hepatocyte necrosis and inflammation due to TRI exposure, because those responses were comparable across the three mouse lines. Significant correlations of ALT and AST responses with NFkappaB-p52 levels underscore the importance of this proinflammatory factor in TRI-induced hepatic damage, as demonstrated previously, although in Pparalpha-null mice, NFkappaB-p65 and -p50 were also elevated after TRI exposure. However, we did not observe substantial differences in ALT, AST, NFkappaB-p52, or TNFalpha levels between mice exposed to the two TRI doses (1,000 and 2,000 ppm), regardless of genotype, and we did not observe dose-related differences in the expression of PPARalpha-target genes in mPPARalpha or hPPARalpha mice. These results, along with evidence that hepatic CYP2E1 expression and levels of TRI metabolites (TCA and TCE) were comparable among the three strains, may be consistent with a role of hepatic CYP2E1 in TRI-induced hepatic damage.

passages.text: Mouse and human PPARalpha were both activated by TRI exposure, but the functional consequences of activation differed substantially between mouse and human PPARalpha, with significantly higher PT and PH mRNA and protein induction by TRI exposure in mPPARalpha than in hPPARalpha mice. Similar results were also observed after exposure to the PPARalpha agonist Wy-14,643. TRI exposure caused significant increases in NFkappaB-p65 and -p50 expression in Pparalpha-null mice but had no effect on either factor in mPPARalpha mice, consistent with complete inhibition of this response by mouse PPARalpha. Human PPARalpha appeared to be less effective in inhibiting this pathway, because TRI exposure did induce significant increases in NFkappaB-p65 expression in hPPARalpha mice. Additionally, we observed comparable levels of the TRI metabolite and PPARalpha ligand TCA in the livers of mPPARalpha and hPPARalpha mice, which suggests that differences are not related to differences in hepatic exposures between the two strains. also reported that human PPARalpha activation by microgram-order perfluorooctanoate, a ligand of PPARalpha, was weaker than mouse PPARalpha activation in response to the same ligand. Taken together, these results suggest functional differences between human and mouse PPARalpha. However, such differences were not observed in a cell transfection study.

There is some evidence that PPARalpha activation inhibits NFkappaB-p65 and p50 and protects against liver injury. Our finding that hepatocyte necrosis and inflammatory cell infiltrations were comparable after TRI exposure in all three mouse strains suggests that PPARalpha might not be important in protecting against the hepatic damage induced by TRI, although we did observe a slight increase in NFkappaB-p65 and -p50 expression after exposure in Pparalpha-null mice. On the other hand, TRI exposure was associated with significant increases in NFkappaB-p52 expression in all three mouse lines, consistent with a previous study and with increased expression of the proinflammatory cytokine TNFalpha. Together, these two factors may then trigger a chain reaction. However, because NFkappaB and TNFalpha mRNA and their proteins were measured using total liver homogenates, we could not distinguish whether the increases were derived from Kupffer cell or hepatocyte responses.

passages.text: The most intriguing result of the present study may be that, although TRI exposure induced enzyme levels involved in the beta-oxidation system to the same degree in both mPPARalpha and hPPARalpha mice, the hepatic TG levels in hPPARalpha mice were increased by TRI exposure in a manner similar to those in Pparalpha-null mice, but not in mPPARalpha mice. Histopathological findings also showed that after TRI exposures, lipid accumulation was increased in hPPARalpha and Pparalpha-null mice compared with mPPARalpha mice. TRI exposure significantly increased the expression of DGAT1 and DGAT2 genes involved in TG synthesis in hPPARalpha but not mPPARalpha mice, suggesting that these genes may contribute to TG accumulation in the livers of TRI-exposed hPPARalpha mice. In Pparalpha-null mice, hepatic TG and lipid accumulation resulting from a lack of PPARalpha-mediated fatty acid catabolism may be exacerbated due to elevated DGAT1 and DGAT2 expression in response to TRI exposure. Hepatic TG and lipid accumulations were observed most clearly in Pparalpha-null mice, followed by hPPARalpha mice, consistent with an important role of TG-synthesizing enzymes in TRI-induced fat accumulation. TRI-induced effects of DGAT1 and DGAT2 appeared to be negatively related to PPARalpha activation. However, PPARgamma was reported to increase expression of these two genes in rats. TRI induced hepatic PPARgamma-mRNA in Pparalpha-null mice, albeit only slightly in hPPARalpha mice and not at all in mPPARalpha mice. Thus, mouse PPARalpha may inhibit the activation of PPARgamma, with the result that PPARgamma may not be induced in the livers of mPPARalpha mice.

Hepatic TG levels were different among the three strains in the absence of TRI exposure, with the highest levels in hPPARalpha mice and the lowest in mPPARalpha mice. This suggests that the human PPARalpha insertion did not restore proper lipid regulation in the liver, but instead resulted in receptor overexpression that exacerbated lipid dysregulation by increasing TG storage and steatosis. Higher constitutive expression of DGAT1 may contribute to these effects, but further experiments are needed to pinpoint the underlying mechanism.

Similar to results in an earlier study, we observed a marked hepatomegaly in mPPARalpha mice exposed to TRI that may be due to cellular hypertrophy resulting from increased numbers of peroxisomes. However, we did not observe cell hypertrophy after TRI exposure in Pparalpha-null and hPPARalpha mice, which suggests that hepatomegaly (as indicated by increased liver/body weight ratios) may have been caused by lipid accumulation rather than peroxisome proliferation. Taken together, the underlying mechanism for TRI-induced hepatomegaly in Pparalpha-null and hPPARalpha mice was different from that in mPPARalpha mice. Although did not observe an increase in liver/body weight ratio after TRI exposure in Pparalpha-null mice, reported a result similar to ours. Discrepancies in the nature of the hepatomegaly caused by TRI exposure may reflect differences in exposure routes, duration, or number of animals used in different studies. We measured the cell proliferation marker PCNA to further investigate hepatocyte proliferation in response to TRI exposure and found that PCNA mRNA increased with TRI exposure in mPPARalpha and hPPARalpha mice but not in Pparalpha-null mice, although PCNA protein expression increased with exposure in three groups. However, we observed histopathological evidence of hepatocyte proliferation in response to TRI exposure in mPPARalpha mice only. This phenomenon should be investigated further.

With regard to TRI metabolism, urinary TCA levels in Pparalpha-null mice were significantly lower than in mPPARalpha mice after TRI exposure. To clarify the mechanism underlying the lower TCA levels, we measured expression of the ALDH2 protein involved in the metabolism of chloral hydrate to TCA because TRI has been reported to inhibit ALDH expression and activity; we found that ALDH2 was reduced to the same degree after TRI exposure in all three strains of mice. reported that the PPARalpha agonist Wy-14,643 also reduced the ALDH2 protein levels by 20-30% in both wild-type and Pparalpha-null mice. Because hepatic ALDH2 protein expression was inhibited by TRI exposure in all three mouse strains, it is an unlikely cause of the decreased urinary levels of TCA in Pparalpha-null mice. Other ALDH isozymes may be involved, and further experiments are therefore needed.

In the present study, the differences in background levels of gene expression between unexposed mPPARalpha and hPPARalpha mice must be duly noted, along with differences in TRI-induced changes in mPPARalpha mice observed between the present study and past studies and discrepancies between mRNA and protein expression for some genes. The replacement of human PPARalpha in this study model may not have been sufficient to prevent steatosis and other effects observed in Pparalpha-null mice; differences in responses between mPPARalpha and hPPARalpha mice may reflect functional consequences related to the use of an artificial construct of the reinserted gene, without normal control elements, in addition to or instead of true functional differences between human and mouse PPARalpha. It also appears that the overexpression of human PPARalpha in this model may lead to greater background toxicity than is present in the Pparalpha-null mice, as indicated by steatosis. We also found differences in gene expression between unexposed mPPARalpha and hPPARalpha mice. Specifically, VLCAD, MCAD, PH, PT, DGAT1, PCNA, p52, and TNFalpha mRNA levels were higher in hPPARalpha mice than in mPPARalpha mice, whereas PH and TNFalpha proteins were comparable, suggesting that mRNA and protein levels do not always correspond with each other, as noted by. Differences in effects of TRI exposure observed between the present and our past study included less-pronounced induction of PPARalpha by TRI exposure and more-pronounced increases in PH protein and VLCAD mRNA expression and ALT and AST levels in response to TRI exposure in our previous study using cyp2e1+/+ mice. We also note that urinary TCA levels for mPPARalpha mice after exposure that we incorrectly reported in our previous study have been corrected here. Therefore, although all elements measured were not completely the same, the two studies are consistent overall. Finally, our study was limited by the small number of mice in each group, which may have limited our power to identify statistically significant biological effects.

passages.text: Conclusions

CYP2E1 appears to be involved in the generation of intermediate metabolites through which TRI induces liver injury in mice. In contrast, PPARalpha, and accordingly PPARgamma, may be important factors in TRI-induced lipid accumulation in the liver. Because we used genetically modified mice with underlying dysregulation and we evaluated very high TRI exposures that proved systemically toxic, our findings may not directly reveal the difference in "human PPARalpha function" as determined between mice and humans. Still, evidence of TRI toxicity independent of PPARalpha status provides valuable information regarding the effects of PPARalpha genetic manipulation.
