passages.text: Comparative hepatotoxicity of a herbicide, epyrifenacil, in humans and rodents by comparing the dynamics and kinetics of its causal metabolite

A new herbicide, epyrifenacil (S-3100), inhibits protoporphyrinogen oxidase (PPO) in plants. Repeated administration of epyrifenacil in laboratory animals led to some toxicological changes related to PPO inhibition, e.g., hepatotoxicity caused by porphyrin accumulation and anemia caused by the inhibition of heme biosynthesis. In vitro studies revealed that an ester-cleaved metabolite, S-3100-CA, is predominant in mammals, exhibits PPO-inhibitory activity, and thus is the cause of epyrifenacil-induced toxicity. To assess the human risk, the effects of species differences on the dynamics (PPO inhibition) and kinetics (liver uptake) of epyrifenacil were evaluated separately. The results of in vitro assays revealed an approximately tenfold weaker inhibition of PPO by S-3100-CA in humans than in rodents and six- to thirteen-fold less hepatic uptake of S-3100-CA in humans than in mice. Finally, it was suggested that humans are less sensitive to the toxicity of epyrifenacil than are rodents, although further mechanistic research is highly anticipated.

passages.text: Introduction

Epyrifenacil (ethyl[(3-{2-chloro-4-fluoro-5-[3-methyl-2,6-dioxo-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3,6-dihydropyrimidin-1(2H)-yl]phenoxy}pyridin-2-yl)oxy]acetate, S-3100) is a new herbicide that acts via the inhibition of protoporphyrinogen oxidase (PPO) in plants. PPO is an essential enzyme involved in the synthesis of chlorophyll in plants. Inhibition of the enzyme in plant cells causes the accumulation of intermediate tetrapyrroles, including protoporphyrin IX (PPIX), and subsequent photoreactions that produce oxygen free radicals to destroy the cell membranes.)

Regarding the toxicity of PPO inhibitors in mammals, similar key events of PPO inhibition and further accumulation of PPIX leading to cell damage may also occur. Thus, it is believed that PPO inhibitors can cause toxicity especially in PPO-generating organs such as the liver and occasionally induce hepatocellular tumors as a consequence of hepatotoxicity.) Additionally, PPO catalyzes the oxidation of protoporphyrinogen IX to PPIX during heme biosynthesis in both plants and mammals. In mammals, the inhibition of PPO blocks the production of hemoglobin and erythrocytes, resulting in anemia.) Since the molecular mechanism of heme biosynthesis is common to all mammals, the possibility that PPO inhibitors are hepatotoxic and/or cause anemia in humans must be considered, especially when such toxicity is observed in rodents and other mammals. However, as is generally recognized, it is impossible to administer a pesticide to humans for toxicological evaluation. On the other hand, it is generally known that species differences in toxicity occur when significant variations in dynamics and kinetics arise among species.) Thus, it was considered very important to evaluate the species differences in the dynamics and kinetics of PPO inhibition separately to precisely assess the risk to humans.

passages.text: For the identification of toxicological profiles including the adverse outcomes related to PPO inhibition, subchronic toxicity studies were conducted for epyrifenacil in some animal species. Since epyrifenacil has an ester bond which is expected to be easily cleavable in mammals, it was considered that epyrifenacil is very rapidly metabolized and the metabolites may work as a causal substance of the toxicity in body. In order to determine the elimination rate of epyrifenacil and to identify the causal metabolites in the body, we conducted an in vitro metabolism study to find a major metabolite and then conducted a PPO-inhibition assay to determine whether the identified metabolite had PPO-inhibitory activity. Lastly, in order to evaluate the risks of epyrifenacil in humans, we focused on species differences in the dynamics (i.e., PPO-inhibitory activity) and kinetics (i.e., exposure, especially hepatic uptake) of the major metabolite.

passages.text: Materials and methods
1. Chemicals

Epyrifenacil (S-3100) and S-3100-CA ((3-{2-chloro-4-fluoro-5-[1,2,3,6-tetrahydro-3-methyl-2,6-dioxo-4-(trifluoromethyl)pyrimidin-1-yl]phenoxy}pyridin-2-yloxy)acetic acid) were synthesized in our laboratory. The chemical purity of these compounds was determined to be 99.8% and 99.7%, respectively, for the in vitro assays. For the subchronic toxicity study, technical-grade epyrifenacil (chemical purity: 96.8%) was used. Pyridyl-4(6)-14C-labeled epyrifenacil was synthesized in our laboratory and had a specific activity of 2.78 GBq/mmol with radiochemical purity of 98.1%. Phenyl-14C-labeled S-3100-CA was also synthesized in our laboratory and had a specific activity of 4.26 GBq/mmol with radiochemical purity of 97.8%. The structures of these compounds are shown in Fig. 1. Krebs-Henseleit buffer (KHB), silicone oil, and mineral oil were purchased from Merck KGaA (Darmstadt, Germany). The hepatocyte isolation kit was supplied by Sekisui XenoTech, LLC (Kansas City, KS, USA). PPIX and sodium amalgam were supplied by Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MI, USA). Other chemicals were of reagent grade.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Fig. 1. Structures of epyrifenacil and its major metabolite, S-3100-CA.
2. Biochemicals

Liver microsomes from male Sprague Dawley (SD) rats (pool of 711), male CD-1 mouse (pool of 1200), and humans (pool of 100 males and 100 females), and liver mitochondrial fractions from SD rats (pool of 15) and humans (pool of 5) were purchased from Sekisui XenoTech, LLC. Liver mitochondrial fractions from mice, rabbits, and dogs were prepared in-house as described later. Cryopreserved primary hepatocytes of male SD rats (pool of 8), female SD rats (pool of 12), male CD-1 mice (pool of 16), and female CD-1 mice (pool of 23) were from Sekisui XenoTech, LLC. Cryopreserved primary hepatocytes of humans (pool of 10 males and 10 females) were purchased from Biopredic International (Saint Gregoire, France).
3. Subchronic toxicity studies with epyrifenacil

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Subchronic (90-day) studies with epyrifenacil in Crl:CD(SD) rats, Crl:CD1(ICR) mice, and beagles were conducted. The design of these studies was based on the relevant test guidelines,) and the studies were conducted in compliance with the principles of Good Laboratory Practice (GLP). All experiments in these studies complied with all applicable sections of the Final Rules of the Animal Welfare Act (Code of Federal Regulations, Title 9),) the Public Health Service Policy on Humane Care and Use of Laboratory Animals from the Office of Laboratory Animal Welfare,) and the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals from the National Research Council.) Detailed study conditions, including animal husbandry, observation and examination items, and toxicokinetics, are presented in the Supplemental Information.

Briefly, rats and mice were dosed with epyrifenacil via dietary administration, and the concentrations of epyrifenacil in the diet were 0 (basal diet only), 50, 300, and 800 ppm in rats and 0, 5, 25, and 100 ppm in mice. Rats and mice were allowed free access to the diet containing epyrifenacil for 90 consecutive days. Dogs were dosed with epyrifenacil in gelatin capsules for 90 consecutive days at dose levels of 0, 100, 300, and 1000 mg/kg/day. The initial day of administration was counted as "Day 0." Animals were randomly distributed into groups consisting of 10 male and 10 female rats and mice, and 4 male and 4 female dogs. Additionally, for toxicokinetic (TK) analyses, 4 male and 4 female rats and 24 male and 24 female mice were allocated to TK satellite groups.
4. In vitro metabolism study of epyrifenacil

An in vitro metabolism study of epyrifenacil was conducted in male rat, male mouse, and human (both genders) liver microsomes. [Pyridyl-4(6)-14C]epyrifenacil (10 microM) was incubated in 100 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.4, containing 1% v/v methanol) with 3 mM NADPH, 3 mM MgCl2, and 1 mg of microsomal protein/mL at 37 C (final volume: 200 microL). The reaction was terminated after 0, 1, 5, 10, and 30 min by adding 200 microL of acetonitrile. Then the samples were vortexed and centrifuged at 20,400xg for 10 min. The supernatant was collected and subjected to HPLC analysis. Radio-HPLC analysis was performed using a Shimadzu LC-20A system (Shimadzu Corporation, Kyoto, Japan) equipped with an L-column 3 ODS (150 mmx4.6 mm, particle size 3 microm, Chemicals Evaluation and Research Institute, Tokyo, Japan). The conditions were as follows: mobile phase, 0.1% formic acid in water (A) and acetonitrile (B); flow rate, 1.0 mL/min; gradient conditions, 20% B at 0 min, 80% B at 20 min, 100% B at 20-23 min, and 20% B at 23-30 min; injection volume, 60 microL; and column oven temperature, 40 C. In an UltimaFlo AP liquid scintillation cocktail (PerkinElmer, Inc., Waltham, MA, USA), the radioactivity of the peaks was measured with an online radio detector, beta-RAM (LabLogic Systems, Ltd., Sheffield, UK).
5. Preparation of liver mitochondrial fractions

For mice, rabbits, and dogs, mitochondrial fractions were prepared in-house using a mitochondrial isolation kit (Cosmo Bio Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) just after the livers were dissected from the animals. Crl:CD1 mice (five 12-week-old males and five 10-week-old females) were purchased from Charles River Laboratories Japan (Kanagawa, Japan). NZW rabbits (five 36-week-old males and six 27- to 32-week-old females) and TOYO beagles (two 7-month-old males and two 7-month-old females) were purchased from Oriental Yeast (Tokyo, Japan). Procedures involving animals and their care conformed to institutional guidelines, which are in compliance with Japanese laws and were approved by the IACUC at our institution.
6. Preparation of protoporphyrinogen IX

In the PPO-inhibition assay, the enzyme activity was evaluated by measuring the amount of PPIX converted from the substrate protoporphyrinogen IX. Since the substrate is unstable and easily oxidized to PPIX, it is not commercially available. Thus, protoporphyrinogen IX was prepared in-house according to the previously described method) with slight modifications. Briefly, approximately 5 mg of PPIX was added to 15 mL of 10 mM KOH containing 20% ethanol and mixed for 20 min in the dark. Then 2.5 mL of the stock solution was mixed with 7.5 mL of 10 mM KOH containing 60 mM ascorbic acid. Next, approximately 5 g of sodium amalgam was gradually added to the reaction mixture under a nitrogen stream. After becoming colorless, the solution was purified using a 0.45 microm cellulose acetate filter to remove the unreacted PPIX. MOPS was added to adjust the pH to ca. 8, and then the solution was stored in liquid nitrogen. Separately, rat mitochondria were used to assay an aliquot of the prepared solution. At plateau fluorescence intensity, the PPIX concentration in the stock was determined to be 35.4 microM.
7. PPO-inhibition assay

The inhibitory activity of the test substances against PPO was measured according to the previously described method.) Assay solutions that contained the test substances and mitochondria at a final concentration of 0.2 mg protein/mL were prepared with 100 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 7.5) containing 0.1% Triton-X, 1 mM EDTA, and 40 mM ascorbic acid and added to a 96-well plate at a volume of 50 microL per well. For the background measurement, which was used to correct for the rate of auto-oxidation of protoporphyrinogen IX, heat-denatured mitochondria (denatured at 80 C for 15 min) were prepared and assayed. After 10 min of preincubation at 37 C in a dry incubator, 50 microL of protoporphyrinogen IX solution was added to each well to achieve a final protoporphyrinogen IX concentration of 0.5 microM. The 96-well plate was loaded into a plate reader (FlexStation3, Molecular Devices, San Jose, CA, USA) prewarmed to 37 C, and the changes in fluorescence (excitation wavelength: 410 nm; emission wavelength: 630 nm) resulting from the conversion to PPIX were monitored for 60 min at 1 min intervals. Separately, 0.25, 0.5, 1, and 2 microM PPIX solutions were prepared to obtain a standard regression line.
8. Calculation of PPO activity

Fluorescence intensity was plotted versus time, and a 10 min linear range was selected for each sample. The amount of produced PPIX was calculated, and the PPO activity was calculated as ng PPIX/min. Vehicle control samples were regarded as full activity controls, and the PPIX production rate obtained from heat-killed mitochondria samples was subtracted as a background. The concentration-response curves were plotted as relative PPO activity (Y, %) versus the logarithm of the test-substance concentration (X, log M). The inhibition curves were fitted to the 4-parameter sigmoidal inhibition model using GraphPad Prism Ver. 5 (GraphPad Software, Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) with weights equal to 1/Y to obtain the IC50 values.
9. Thawing of cryopreserved primary hepatocytes

Cryopreserved primary hepatocytes were thawed according to the hepatocyte isolation kit instructions. Briefly, the hepatocytes were thawed in a water bath at 37 C and immediately transferred to a tube containing 25 mL of thawing medium warmed to 37 C. Cells were centrifuged at 100xg for 5 min at r.t. to remove the supernatant and then resuspended in 2 mL of KHB (containing 118 mM NaCl, 23.8 mM NaHCO3, 4.8 mM KCl, 1.0 mM KH2PO4, 1.2 mM MgSO4, 12.5 mM HEPES, 5.0 mM glucose, and 1.5 mM CaCl2, adjusted to pH 7.4) at 4 C. To remove the thawing medium completely, cells were centrifuged at 100xg for 5 min at r.t., the supernatant was removed again, and the cells were resuspended in 2 mL of KHB at 4 C. Cell concentration was measured and adjusted to 2.0x106 cells/mL.
10. Hepatocyte uptake assay

A hepatocyte uptake assay was conducted using the previously described method with modifications.) In short, the cells were incubated in a medium containing radiolabeled S-3100-CA and finally separated on the basis of difference in specific gravity using an oil layer of intermediate density. An aliquot (100 microL) of each suspension of cryopreserved primary hepatocytes (2.0x106 cells/mL) was pre-incubated for 5 min at 37 C or 4 C (on ice). The uptake assay was initiated by adding an equal volume of [phenyl-14C]S-3100-CA solution (final concentration: 5 microM) in KHB. After incubation at 37 C or 4 C, 100 microL of each culture solution was transferred into a microcentrifuge tube containing 100 microL of 2 N NaOH under 100 microL of the oil layer (silicone oil/mineral oil=81.7/18.3, v/v; density: 1.016 g/mL). Next, the uptake was terminated at 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 min after the start of incubation by centrifuging the tube at 20,400xg for 1.0 min at 4 C to transfer the cells from the upper culture solution to the bottom NaOH layer. After the centrifugation, each tube was stored overnight at 50 C to allow dissolution of the cells in the NaOH layer. Each tube was frozen at -80 C and cut at the oil layer using a tube cutter. Aliquots of the NaOH layer were transferred into a scintillation vial, and 10 mL of scintillation cocktail, Hionic-Fluor  (PerkinElmer, Inc., Waltham, MA, USA), was added. The radioactivity in the cell lysate was measured by liquid scintillation counting (LSC, Tri-Carb  3110TR, PerkinElmer, Inc.).
11. Calculation of hepatic uptake volume

The total radioactivity in the NaOH layer [dpm/105 cells] was divided by the radioactivity concentration in the culture solution [dpm/mL] to obtain the volume of substrate uptake in the hepatocytes [microL/106 cells]. The active uptake volume was defined as the difference in uptake volume between 37 C and 4 C, and then the time-dependent increase in the active uptake volume was transformed into the rate of S-3100-CA active uptake by hepatocytes (active uptake rate).
Results
1. Subchronic study

Detailed results of the 90-day subchronic studies conducted in rats, mice, and dogs are presented in the Supplemental Information, and the summary results are presented in Table 1. Briefly, 90-day subchronic toxicity studies in mice, rats, and dogs showed similar profiles of toxicity, which were limited to anemia and hepatotoxicity. Similar anemic changes were noted in all species tested. Regarding hepatotoxicity, hepatocyte injury, which was mainly characterized by hepatocellular degeneration/necrosis and/or single-cell necrosis/apoptosis, was observed in both rats and mice, but dogs did not show the alterations indicative of evident hepatocyte injury. Among the three species tested, the mice showed the lowest NOAEL based on anemia and/or hepatotoxicity, followed by the rats and then the dogs. In all species, males tended to be more susceptible than females.

2. Toxicokinetics

The toxicokinetics data obtained in the subchronic study is presented in Table S4 and summarized in Table 2. The exposure to the metabolite (S-3100-CA) increased as the dose increased, in terms of AUC0-24 and Cmax, in a nearly dose-proportional manner in all species tested, whereas no parent epyrifenacil was detected. There were no notable differences in exposure to S-3100-CA between males and females. Furthermore, there was no accumulation of S-3100-CA following 90 days of oral administration of epyrifenacil to all species tested. Only a limited amount of the parent epyrifenacil was detected in dog plasma (not more than 0.04 microg/mL), whereas no measurable amount was detected in rats or mice (data not shown), suggesting that a majority of epyrifenacil was converted to S-3100-CA in all species tested.

3. In vitro metabolism study

In order to determine the elimination rate of epyrifenacil and to identify the major metabolites in rodents and humans, we conducted an in vitro metabolism study. The result is shown in Fig. 2. When incubated with microsomal fractions, epyrifenacil was rapidly metabolized and almost disappeared within 5 min in all species tested. As a major metabolite, S-3100-CA was detected with no less than 80% of the applied radioactivity. No quantitative or qualitative difference in the production of the metabolite was observed among rats, mice, or humans in this experiment. To evaluate the contribution of the non-enzymatic reaction, epyrifenacil was assayed without microsomal fractions, which did not present any degradants after 30 min of incubation.
Fig. 2. Percent in samples of epyrifenacil  and S-3100-CA  after incubation of [14C]epyrifenacil with rat (left), mouse (center), and human (right) microsomal fractions.
4. PPO-inhibition assay

To investigate the inhibitory activity of epyrifenacil and its major metabolite S-3100-CA against PPO, an in vitro enzyme-inhibition assay of test substances in mitochondrial fractions from mouse, rat, rabbit, dog, and human livers was conducted. The results are shown in Fig. 3, and the calculated IC50 values are presented in Table 3. When the inhibitory activities of epyrifenacil and S-3100-CA were compared, the IC50 values were approximately the same for each species, but especially in mice, S-3100-CA was slightly stronger than the parent compound. This result suggests that hydrolysis of the ethyl ester did not reduce the PPO-inhibitory potential. When compared among the species, the IC50 values were comparable in mice and rats. However, the PPO-inhibitory activity in dogs, rabbits, and humans was 3- to 5-fold smaller for epyrifenacil and 7- to 14-fold smaller for S-3100-CA than that in mice and rats, suggesting the existence of a significant difference in the dynamics of PPO inhibition between rodents and other species, including humans.

5. Hepatocyte uptake assay

The active hepatic uptake of S-3100-CA was evaluated using hepatocytes of rodents and humans. The results are summarized in Fig. 4. In all species tested, the uptake volume of S-3100-CA was larger at 37 C, which includes the volume of active uptake via hepatic transporters, than at 4 C, which includes the volume of uptake by passive diffusion and cell surface adsorption. Therefore, it was suggested that S-3100-CA is taken up into hepatocytes by the hepatic transporters of all tested species. The active uptake volume (active uptake clearance, hereafter abbreviated as CL) was increased in a time-dependent manner. Comparing CL values among the species, the largest was in male mice, followed in order by those in female mice, male rats, female rats, and humans (both genders). From the CL values obtained, the rate of active S-3100-CA uptake in each species was determined during a time interval when the CL increased linearly with good repeatability (i.e., male rat, female rat, and human: 0.5 to 2.0 min; male mouse: 0.25 to 2.0 min; female mouse: 0.25 to 1.0 min). The calculated uptake rates are presented in Fig. 5. The uptake rate in the hepatocytes of humans (3.83 microL/106 cells/min) was significantly lower than that in the hepatocytes of male mice (49.51 microL/106 cells/min), female mice (21.58 microL/106 cells/min), and male rats (8.10 microL/106 cells/min) and tended to be lower than that in female rats (6.66 microL/106 cells/min), although the difference was not statistically significant. When the uptake was compared between males and females of the same species, uptake was significantly higher in male mice, while in male rats, it was higher but not statistically significant.

Discussion

As mentioned above, PPO inhibitors can cause hepatotoxicity stemming from the accumulation of PPIX in hepatocytes) and anemic changes due to the inhibition of heme biosynthesis.) Hepatotoxicity caused by epyrifenacil in rodents was characterized by hepatocellular degeneration/necrosis and/or single-cell necrosis/apoptosis, which were associated with bile duct hyperplasia in rats or brown pigment deposition in Kupffer cells in mice, as summarized in Table S2. It has been reported that the administration of porphyrogenic compounds to rodents induces the accumulation of a porphyrin-containing pigment in combination with hepatocyte injury,) which is observed as dark brown to red-brown pigment deposition in hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, and portal macrophages,) and also in bile ducts, leading to bile duct proliferation.) These pathologic natures were clearly in line with the histopathological findings observed in the subchronic studies with epyrifenacil and other PPO inhibitors.) In contrast to the above results in rodents, the hepatotoxicity observed in dogs was limited to increased glycogen and an associated increase in ALP, which was not suggestive of porphyrin accumulation. Furthermore, subchronic studies identified the hematopoietic system as the target of epyrifenacil in all species tested, as characterized by decreases in RBC, HGB, HCT, MCH, MCV, and/or MCHC, and associated findings indicative of increased erythropoiesis. These alterations were clearly in line with the reports about other PPO inhibitors) and thus were attributed to PPO inhibition and the subsequent disruption of heme biosynthesis. From these results, the adverse outcomes caused by epyrifenacil in rats and mice were determined to be limited to hepatotoxicity and anemia, both derived from PPO inhibition. As presented in Table 1, males tended to be more susceptible to these toxicological effects than females across species. The reason has not been identified, but an in vitro hepatocyte assay revealed the higher uptake of S-3100-CA in the male liver especially in mice, suggesting that sex differences in the exposure of S-3100-CA to the main target organ (i.e., the liver) might cause the higher toxicity in males.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: As presented in Fig. 1, epyrifenacil has an ester bond in its structure, which is expected to cleave easily and thereby produce S-3100-CA. In order to identify the major metabolites in the body and to estimate the species differences in exposure to metabolites, we conducted an in vitro metabolism study with liver microsomal fractions. The results showed that the ester cleavage in epyrifenacil was very rapid in all species tested, suggesting that epyrifenacil is mostly metabolized by the first-pass effect when dosed orally. In addition, the ester-cleaved metabolite, S-3100-CA, was predominant and commonly detected. A metabolism study using 14C-labeled epyrifenacil was conducted separately); S-3100-CA was detected as a major metabolite in the plasma of rats and mice, whereas no conjugate of S-3100-CA was detected in urine or feces of rats. In addition, approximately half the amount of dosed 14C was excreted as S-3100-CA into urine and feces, suggesting that the renal and biliary excretion takes a significant part of the rate-limiting process for the elimination of S-3100-CA; conversely, the predominant circulating metabolite in the body is S-3100-CA.) Combining these observations with the in vitro data above, it was expected that S-3100-CA would be the major component in mice and rats, and probably also in humans. In order to conclude that it was the main cause of epyrifenacil-induced hepatotoxicity in rodents, we also conducted an in vitro PPO-inhibition assay. The results showed that S-3100-CA inhibited PPO in rodents, and the extent of inhibition was similar to that by the parent epyrifenacil. From these results, we concluded that the major causal substance of epyrifenacil-induced hepatotoxicity in rodents is S-3100-CA.

Since the molecular mechanism of heme biosynthesis is common to all mammals, the possibility of PPO-inhibitor-induced hepatotoxicity and/or anemia in humans should be taken into consideration for the human-health-risk assessment of epyrifenacil. For precise risk assessment, we planned to look for evidence of species differences in the dynamics (i.e., PPO-inhibitory activity) and kinetics (i.e., uptake by the liver) of PPO inhibition separately. Analysis of the PPO-inhibition assay results showed a significant species difference. When focused on S-3100-CA, the IC50 in humans was 8.3 times greater than that in rats and 13.9 times greater than that in mice, demonstrating that the sensitivity to PPO inhibition by S-3100-CA is lower in humans than in rodents. The IC50 values in dogs and rabbits were almost equal to those in humans. When comparing the NOAELs in the tested species based on hepatotoxicity and anemia, the mouse was the most sensitive species, followed by the rat and then the dog, which is consistent with the difference in sensitivity to PPO inhibition. These PPO-inhibition results suggested that dogs were the most relevant species to humans, but the reference values of epyrifenacil for risk assessment (e.g., acceptable daily intake or acceptable operator-exposure level) are most likely to be derived from the mouse studies, ensuring that these reference values are protective of human health. The details underlying species differences have not been revealed. Regarding the molecular dynamics toward PPO, a docking simulation study of the PPO inhibitor flumioxazin in several species clearly demonstrated that the binding affinity of the substrate to PPO varies among species.) There are no direct data or literatures available, but it is estimated that a similar variation of the binding affinity among species is also occurred for S-3100-CA.

Regarding the kinetics, the in vitro metabolism data showed no quantitative or qualitative difference in the production or metabolic degradation of S-3100-CA among the species. As shown in Fig. 1, S-3100-CA contains a carboxylic acid moiety, which is highly likely to be ionized and to exist as a COO- anion under physiological conditions. It is known that such anions are sometimes taken up into organs via organic anion transporters (OATs) or organic anion transporting peptides (OATPs) and cause significant exposure to the chemicals.) Furthermore, it has been reported that there are species differences in the active transport of chemicals and thereby species differences in exposure and toxicity.) When considering the target organs of epyrifenacil, the active transport is mainly contributed to the liver rather than the hemopoietic system, and thus we focused on evaluating species differences in the hepatic uptake of S-3100-CA. The results of in vitro assays using hepatocytes from rodents and humans demonstrated that the uptake of S-3100-CA is 6 to 13 times greater in mice and 2 times greater in rats than in humans. This result clearly indicates that exposure to S-3100-CA in the liver is lower in humans than in rodents, especially mice. Therefore, it was concluded that the risk of hepatotoxicity by S-3100-CA in humans is lower than that in rodents based on species differences in both dynamics and kinetics. Another proposal that involves the contribution of OATPs is the notable sex-related difference in the uptake of S-3100-CA. It has already been reported that the expression of some OATPs is significantly higher in the liver of male mice and male rats,) whereas no sex-related difference in OATPs has been noted in humans.) These previous studies are likely to explain the sex-related difference in S-3100-CA uptake observed in rodents. Our research provides only phenomenological results, and thus further mechanistic research to explain the significant difference between species or sexes is highly anticipated.

passages.text: From these results, it was suggested that humans are significantly less sensitive to the hepatotoxicity of epyrifenacil than are rodents, and this difference stems from species differences in the dynamics and/or kinetics of the causal metabolite, S-3100-CA. The findings of this research were considered to enable an interpretation of the species differences between rodents and humans and provide a robust basis for the human-health-risk assessment of epyrifenacil, though further mechanistic research of species differences is highly expected.

passages.text: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) inhibit cytochrome P450 CYP3A7 through direct coordination to the heme iron and water displacement

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are a chemical class of highly stable, fluorinated compounds popular for use in a variety of consumer products. PFAS environmental persistence in drinking water contributes to acute exposure in humans and subsequent bioaccumulation of the compounds in the liver and lung tissue. Prenatal PFAS exposure has been associated with lowered birth weight, premature birth, and developmental defects including cranio-facial abnormalities. The cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP3A7 is responsible for facilitating a variety of reactions essential for proper fetal development in humans. In addition to drug metabolism, CYP3A7 is responsible for metabolizing endogenous ligands in the developing human liver, including the steroid precursor dehydroepiandrosterone 3-sulfate (DHEA-S), essential for estriol synthesis during pregnancy, along with the morphogen all-trans-retinoic acid (atRA). Interference with estriol synthesis during pregnancy, as well as atRA clearance, is known to result in similar effects associated with prenatal PFAS exposure including lowered birth weight, premature birth, and developmental defects. We hypothesized that PFAS compounds bind to the CYP3A7 enzyme resulting in its inhibition. We implemented a series of binding studies using spectral characterization of six PFAS compounds (PFOA, PFOS, GenX, PFNA, PFNS, and PFHxS), and evaluated their interactions with recombinant CYP3A7. In addition, we screened PFAS for their ability to inhibit CYP3A7 oxidative activity using dibenzylfluorescein, a fluorescent probe, and DHEA-S, an endogenous substrate of CYP3A7. Our data demonstrate that of the six PFAS tested, PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, and PFHxS bind to and inhibit CYP3A7.
Graphical Abstract:

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) coordinate with the heme iron in the CYP3A7 active site and displace water resulting in both reverse Type I and Type I binding. These unique interactions feature negative cooperativity related to PFAS concentration and propensity for electrostatic repulsion, resulting in inhibition of CYP3A7 oxidative activity.
INTRODUCTION

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are a chemical class of over 4,700 fluorinated aliphatic compounds known for their oleophobic and hydrophobic qualities. Their physicochemical stability makes them popular for use in a vast multitude of consumer products including disposable food and toy packaging, clothing, carpeting, and cookware. PFAS are also major components of aqueous film-forming foams (AFFF), which belong to a category of flame retardants often used at airports and military bases for training purposes. These compounds can leach or shed from consumer products into food, air, and soil leading to background human exposure. In addition, runoff from manufacturing plants, airports and military bases into local waterways serves as the main source for chronic PFAS exposure in humans, as we currently lack the proper infrastructure to filter these environmentally persistent compounds from consumer water.

Their remarkable resilience to degradation pathways has been attributed to the strong carbon-fluorine (C-F) bonds in PFAS alkyl chains, which explains their widespread prevalence in human tissues with half-lives reaching 5 years. Legacy compounds with longer alkyl chains such as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorosulfonic acid (PFOS) have been manufactured since the 1940s and have been thoroughly studied in the literature. Findings of associations between these compounds and adverse health effects has led to their gradual ban in signatory countries by the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs). These legacy compounds have since been replaced by novel shorter-chain compounds such as hexafluoropropylene oxide-dimer acid (HFPO-DA, or GenX) with six carbons in its alkyl chain (Figure 1). Although it has been argued that substitutes for legacy compounds are more biologically inert, it has been observed in recent animal models that these novel compounds possess similar or higher toxic potency than their predecessors. Legacy compounds remain ubiquitous in nearly 98% of human serum in the United States and maintain their relevancy in the scientific literature despite their phase-out. Further research is necessary to compare the biochemical properties and subsequent health effects of the two classes, to either confirm or deny these claims.

PFAS exposure in humans is associated with a variety of health effects including immunosuppression, as well as endocrine and metabolic disruption. First exposure to PFAS can start as early as the in-utero period via maternal umbilical cord blood. In the human embryo, these compounds have been found to bioaccumulate in the lungs during the first trimester of development and in the liver during the second and third trimesters of development. PFAS can additionally be transferred from mother to infant through breast milk after birth, and formula-fed infants remain exposed through their intake of public drinking water. Prenatal PFAS exposure is associated with preterm birth, lowered birth weight, and developmental defects such as craniofacial abnormalities.

The human hepatic cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme CYP3A7 comprises nearly half the CYP content in the neonatal and fetal liver. CYP3A7 is expressed primarily during fetal development and up to 12 months after birth performing many of the same functions as its adult isoform CYP3A4, with which it shares 87% of its genetic sequence. In addition to drug metabolism, CYP3A7 is responsible for metabolism of endogenous compounds such as dehydroepiandrostenedione 3-sulfate (DHEA-S) which it hydroxylates into 16alpha-hydroxy-DHEA-S. This is a key step in the estriol biosynthetic pathway during pregnancy. Estriol synthesis up-regulates uterine vasodilation and is necessary to bring a pregnancy to full-term. In addition to metabolism of DHEA-S, CYP3A7 is one of the CYP enzymes responsible for clearance of all-trans-retinoic acid (atRA), a metabolite of vitamin A1, from the developing liver. Improper clearance of atRA results in accumulation and subsequent hepatotoxicity. High levels of atRA in the neonatal and fetal liver have been associated with teratogenicity resulting in developmental defects such as cranio-facial abnormalities, as well as spontaneous abortion.

The promiscuous substrate specificity of the CYP3A isoforms predispose them to interactions with ligand mimickers that share structural resemblance with endogenous ligands. PFAS compounds not only possess long alkyl chains similar to those of fatty acids, but certain PFAS have identical functional groups to those of known CYP3A7 ligands (Figure 1). PFOS, perfluorononanesulfonic acid (PFNS), and perfluorohexane sulfonic acid (PFHxS), all prominent PFAS in the literature, possess sulfonic acid head groups such as that of DHEA-S. Additionally, PFOA, GenX, and perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA) each contain carboxylic acid head groups comparable to that of atRA (Figure 1). Given these chemical resemblances, there is a propensity in the CYP3A7 binding site for low-affinity interactions with these familiar functional groups found on PFAS.

These potential interactions may lead to subsequent inhibition of CYP3A7 activity by PFAS compounds. Previous studies have shown PFAS inhibition of other CYP enzymes involved in steroid and lipid synthesis including CYP2C19, CYP2E1, and CYP2D6, as well as CYP3A4. However, interactions between PFAS and CYP3A7 are not well characterized. Given the similarities in the literature between the effects of prenatal PFAS exposure and those related to inhibition of estriol synthesis and atRA clearance, we hypothesized that PFAS compounds can bind to and inhibit CYP3A7.

We performed binding studies to determine the specific interactions between CYP3A7 and six prominent PFAS in the literature (PFOA, PFOS, GenX, PFNA, PFNS, and PFHxS). CYP enzymes largely display characteristic absorbance spectra which can be used to monitor ligand binding. The type of spectra represents the specific interactions that take place between a ligand and the heme iron in the binding pocket of the CYP enzyme. Typical CYP absorbance spectra are grouped into three different categories: Type I, reverse Type I, or Type II. Spectra are classified based on unique properties related to absorbance values at different wavelengths, and the overall shape of the curve. Type I and reverse Type I spectra are both indicative of a displacement of water by the ligand in the CYP's binding pocket. However, during reverse Type I binding, there is an additional interaction between a heteroatom from the ligand (e.g., oxygen or sulfur), with the heme iron in the binding site of the CYP. This results in spectra which mirror that of Type I spectra, reflected across the x-axis. Type II absorbance spectra occur as a result of a nitrogen atom on a ligand coordinating with the CYP's heme iron and forming a covalent bond. Given that none of the PFAS tested possess a nitrogen atom, we expected to observe either Type I or reverse Type I spectra when characterizing these interactions. Our observations were verified through molecular docking studies.

Additionally, the PFAS that were shown to interact with CYP3A7 were screened for their ability to inhibit the oxidative activity of the enzyme. The data obtained from these experiments provide insight into the biochemical mechanisms leading to developmental toxicity resulting from prenatal PFAS exposure.

passages.text: MATERIALS AND METHODS
Chemicals.

Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was purchased from Alfa Aesar (Haverhill, MA). PFOA (CAS: 335-95-5) was purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc. (Waltham, MA). PFOS (CAS: 2795-39-3) was supplied by Sigma-Aldrich (St Louis, MO). GenX (CAS: 62037-80-3) was purchased from Manchester Organics (Runcorn, UK). PFNA (CAS: 375-95-1) and PFHxS (CAS: 3871-99-6) were both acquired through Frontier Scientific Inc. (Logan, UT). PFNS (CAS: 98789-57-2) was purchased from Toronto Research Chemicals (Toronto, ON). All PFAS stocks were prepared fresh in DMSO prior to each experiment (5-100 mM). Glucose-6-phosphate, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, beta-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP+), and dehydroepiandrosterone-d5-3-sulfate (DHEA-S-d5) were all purchased from Sigma Aldrich (St. Louis, MO). The fluorescent probe substrate, dibenzylfluorescein (DBF, CAS: 97744-44-0) and DHEA-S (CAS: 1099-87-2) were supplied by Cayman Chemical Company (Ann Arbor, MI). The metabolite standard, 16alpha-hydroxy DHEA-S, was purchased from Steraloids (Newport, RI). The CYP3A7 Bactosomes (catalog number: CYP/EZ060) were purchased from Cypex Ltd. (Scotland, UK) where the recombinant CYP3A7 enzyme was co-expressed with the human cytochrome P450 reductase in E. coli and then supplemented with the human cytochrome b5.
Recombinant CYP3A7 Protein Expression.

Recombinant human CYP3A7 (rCYP3A7) was expressed and purified based on the protocol outlined by Godamudunage et al.. An N-terminally truncated, codon-optimized, and His-tagged CYP3A7 cDNA cloned into the pCWori+ vector (pCWori-CYP3A7d4-24H4) was a generous gift from the Dr. Emily Scott Lab (Department of Medicinal Chemistry, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA). The construct was designed for expression in chemically competent Escherichia coli DH5alpha F'IQ cells (Thermo-Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) that have been previously transformed with the pGro7 chaperone plasmid (Emily Scott Lab). Transformation of E. coli DH5alpha/pGro7 cells with pCWori-CYP3A7d4-24H4 was achieved via heat shock and grown overnight at 37 C on Luria Broth (LB) plates containing chloramphenicol (20 mug/mL) and ampicillin (100 mug/mL). CYP3A7 was expressed under the control of the tac promoter of the pCWOri+ plasmid using E. coli-DH5alpha F'IQ cells (Thermo-Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) in Terrific Broth (TB) medium. Briefly, 20 mL of an overnight pCWori-CYP3A7 E. coli-DH5alpha starter culture consisting of LB medium supplemented with 20 mug/mL chloramphenicol and 200 mug/mL ampicillin was used to inoculate each liter of TB (also containing 20 mug/mL chloramphenicol and 200 mug/mL ampicillin). The bacterial cultures were incubated in 2.8L PYREX Erlenmeyer Flasks (Charleroi, PA; No. 4420) at 37 C under agitation until the optical density reached an absorbance at 600 nm of 0.5. Upon reaching 0.5 OD600, the GroES/EL chaperone expression was induced by adding arabinose (2 mg/mL) and 1 mM delta-aminolaevulinic acid was also added at that time. The incubation temperature was reduced to 25 C under agitation until reaching an OD600 of 0.6-0.8. At that optical density, CYP3A7 expression was induced by the addition of 1 mM isopropyl ss-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG). Following induction, cells were grown for 48 h at 25 C under agitation, then were harvested via centrifugation at 2,400 x g at 4 C. Cells were further processed to spheroplasts by resuspending them in lysis buffer [20 mM TrisHCl (pH 8.0), 20% glycerol, 1 mM PMSF, 10 mM beta -mercaptoethanol] while adding chicken egg white lysozyme (Millipore-Sigma, St. Louis, MO) at 0.3 mg/mL and stirring at 4 C for 30 min. Lysed cells were centrifuged for 15 min at 8,300 x g at 4 C, and the spheroplast pellet was collected and stored at -80 C until ready for purification of the expressed CYP3A7 enzyme.
Recombinant (His)-Tagged CYP3A7 Protein Purification.

Spheroplast pellets were thawed at room temperature and resuspended in cold buffer consisting of 20 mM TrisHCl (pH 8.0), 20% glycerol, 1 mM PMSF, 10 mM beta-mercaptoethanol. The spheroplast suspension was then lysed on ice with a Branson sonicator set at 100% power and five 30-sec bursts with 30-sec resting time between each burst. The lysate was then centrifugated for 15 min at 8,300 x g and 4 C to remove spheroplast debris. The resulting supernatant underwent ultra-centrifugation for 45 min at 100,000 x g and 4 C. The pellet obtained was then homogenized in buffer consisting of 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8, 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM PMSF, 5 mM beta-mercaptoethanol, and 20% glycerol. To help the solubilization of CYP3A7, 1% 3-((3-cholamidopropyl) dimethylammonio)-1-propanesulfonate (CHAPS) was gradually added and stirred up to 2 h at 4 C. The mixture was finally ultra-centrifugated for 50 min at 100,000 x g and 4 C. The CYP3A7-containing supernatant was loaded onto a Ni-NTA HisTrap-HP column (Cytiva, Marlborough, MA) pre-equilibrated with the loading buffer consisting of 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8, 500 mM NaCl, 10 mM imidazole, 10 mM CHAPS, and 20% glycerol. The column was subsequently washed with five column volumes (CV) of loading buffer, followed by 5 CV of wash buffer (100 mM potassium phosphate pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 10 mM imidazole, 10 mM CHAPS, and 20% glycerol). rCYP3A7 was then eluted with a gradient of imidazole using the elution buffer of 10 mM potassium phosphate pH 7.4, 100 mM NaCl, 250 mM imidazole, 10 mM CHAPS. Red colored fractions were pooled and diluted 5-fold with the carboxymethyl (CM) wash buffer consisting of 5 mM potassium phosphate pH 7.4, 1 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), 6 mM CHAPS, and 20% glycerol. The diluted pooled sample was loaded on a HiTrap CM sepharose FF column (Cytiva, Marlborough, MA) and then washed with ten column volumes of CM wash buffer. The rCYP3A7 protein was eluted based with a 10 CV salt-gradient using the elution buffer of 50 mM potassium phosphate, pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, and 20% glycerol. The CM sepharose fractions containing the bulk of the rCYP3A7 protein were pooled, concentrated, and dialyzed at 4 C in 100 mM potassium phosphate pH 7.4, 1 mM EDTA, 0.1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), and 20% glycerol. The final protein concentration of the purified rCYP3A7 was determined by bicinchoninic acid assay (Pierce, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The final concentration of the ferrous-CO protein was determined using UV-visible spectroscopy on an Agilent Cary 60 spectrophotometer (Agilent Technologies; Santa Clara, CA), with an extinction coefficient of epsilon = 91 mM-1 cm-1 at the wavelength of 450 nm.
Optical Difference Spectroscopy of PFAS Binding to rCYP3A7.

UV-visible difference spectroscopy studies were performed on an Agilent Cary 60 spectrophotometer (Agilent Technologies; Santa Clara, CA). Binding of PFOA [10 to 600 muM], PFOS [2.5 to 200 muM], GenX [2.5 to 600 muM], PFNA [10 to 700 muM], PFNS [2.5 to 300 muM], and PFHxS [50 to 1500 muM] to CYP3A7 were tested (n=3). Positive controls for Type I (Lopinavir [0.25 to 20 muM]) and Type II (Ketoconazole [0.25 to 150 muM]) binding were acquired for comparison (n=1). Concentration ranges used were optimized based on data from preliminary screening. All stock solutions were prepared and diluted by serial dilution in DMSO. Both sample and reference chambers contained 1 mL of rCYP3A7 (2 muM for PFAS; 1 muM for controls) in 100 mM potassium phosphate (pH 7.4). Prior to initiating the titration, a baseline was recorded between 350 and 500 nm. Aliquots of ligand solutions were added to the sample cuvette, whereas equal volume of DMSO was added to the reference cuvette to determine the difference spectrum at varying PFAS concentrations. The absolute changes in absorbance deriving from triplicate titrations were plotted as a function of ligand concentration. The dissociation constant (Kd), R2, and Bmax for each ligand was calculated with the nonlinear regression Hill (h) equation (equation 1) using GraphPad Prism 9 for MacOS (version 9.4.1) (San Diego, CA).  Where Y is the fraction of the receptor protein (CYP) concentration that is bound by the ligand, X is the total ligand concentration, Bmax is the absolute spectral response, and h is the Hill coefficient.
In-Silico Docking Studies of PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, and PFHxS to CYP3A7.

Molecular docking studies were performed for the four PFAS compounds binding to CYP3A7: PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, and PFHxS using AutoDock Vina v. 1.1.2. Studies were performed using the experimental crystal dimer structure of fetal-specific CYP3A7 (PDB: 7MK8) from Sevrioukova et al. downloaded from the Protein Data Bank (PDB: https://www.rcsb.org/). The receptor was prepared for docking by removing ions and water molecules and adding polar hydrogens using MGL AutoDock Tools v 1.5.7 (UCSD Molecular Graphics Lab and The Scripps Research Institute). PFAS 3D structures were downloaded from PubChem (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), converted to PDB, and parameterized by adding polar hydrogens and identifying rotatable bonds. Coordinates for the receptor docking grid search space were established by defining the enzyme active site, with the following parameters: grid box center: x-center = 93.937, y-center = 284.197, z-center = 174.386, and total number of grid points in each direction: x-dimension = y-dimension = z-dimension = 30. A configuration docking script was prepared using MS Notepad in text format with the exhaustiveness search parameter set to 24. AutoDock Vina was executed using the configuration file with PDBQT.out and log.out file options included. The PDBQT.out file contains all binding poses for any particular docking simulation. Output files were analyzed using the ViewDock feature in UCSF Chimera v. 1.15. Docking energies and associated distances (A) between each heteroatom (reverse Type I) or omega-1 carbon (Type I) interaction for each PFAS were recorded (Table 2). Relevant docking poses were selected based on energetic favorability and proximity to the heme iron.
PFAS in vitro Inhibition Screening Assay for Recombinant CYP3A7 using the DBF Probe Substrate.

PFAS compounds which exhibited successful binding to rCYP3A7 were evaluated for their capacity to inhibit CYP3A7 bactosome activity using DBF as a fluorescent probe substrate. CYP3A7 bactosomes were implemented instead of purified rCYP3A7 to more faithfully recapitulate kinetics in vivo. Experimental setup was based on the DBF high-throughput assay previously described in Work et al.. In brief, PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, and PFHxS stocks (5 and 50 mM) were prepared fresh daily in DMSO and combined with the DBF-recombinant CYP3A7 (0.15 muM DBF; 10 pmol/mL CYP3A7 bactosomes) incubations done in 0.1 M potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) and 3.3 mM magnesium chloride to yield a 10 and 100 muM PFAS final concentrations, respectively. DMSO was used for solvent control and did not exceed 0.2% final concentration across reactions to minimize non-specific CYP interactions. Reactions (final volume of 100 muL), in triplicate, were initiated at 37 C by the addition of the NADPH-regenerating system mix consisting of NADP+ (1 mM), glucose-6-phosphate (10 mM), and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (2 IU/mL) and were stopped by the addition of 75 muL 2 M NaOH. After 1 h incubation of the stopped samples at 37 C, formation of the fluorescent metabolite of DBF, fluorescein, was measured using a Tecan Infinite M Plex microplate reader (Mannedorf, Switzerland) to determine CYP3A7 activity. Additional incubations without the NADPH-regenerating system mix were done in parallel as negative controls. The solvent control samples were used as reference for 100% activity to calculate the percent inhibition in samples containing the PFAS compounds. The GraphPad Prism 9 software for MacOS (version 9.4.1) was used for data processing, graph generation and descriptive statistics (San Diego, CA).
PFAS IC50 Inhibition Assays for Recombinant CYP3A7 and DBF Oxidation.

PFAS compounds that achieved over 50% inhibition in the CYP3A7 inhibition screening assay (PFOS and PFNA) were further characterized for their inhibition properties by carrying out IC50 assays. Similar experimental procedure as the screening assay was followed. PFOS (80 mM) and PFNA (150 mM) stock solutions were prepared in DMSO and working solutions were made by serial dilution in DMSO to yield final PFOS and PFNA concentrations in incubations ranging from 1.25 to 160 muM and 2.5 to 300 muM, respectively. DMSO was used as the solvent control and did not exceed 0.2% final concentration across reactions to prevent non-specific CYP interactions. Percent remaining activities with increasing PFAS concentrations were calculated based on the initial velocity of the formation of the DBF metabolite, fluorescein, against the solvent control. The half maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC50) for each PFAS were determined based on the dose-response curve fitting using the log(inhibitor) vs. response - variable slope (equation 2) from GraphPad Prism 9 software for MacOS (version 9.4.1) (San Diego, CA).
PFOS IC50 Inhibition Assay for Recombinant CYP3A7 and DHEA-S Hydroxylation.

Since PFOS had the lowest IC50 value for CYP3A7 DBF oxidation, it was further characterized for its in vitro inhibition potency for CYP3A7 DHEA-S hydroxylation. The IC50 assay was performed according to the procedure previously outlined in Kandel et al. with the following modifications: PFOS stock and working solutions were prepared in DMSO at the concentrations previously described for the DBF oxidation assay and CYP3A7 Bactosome reactions (10 pmol/mL) were incubated up to 5 min at 37 C. After removal of precipitated proteins by centrifugation, supernatant samples were analyzed by LC-MS/MS for formation of the 16alpha-hydroxy DHEA-S metabolite according to the analytical method described in Kandel et al. and using the Xevo TQ-S micro tandem quadrupole mass spectrometer (Waters Corp. Milford, MA) with multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) scan type. The MS peaks were integrated using QuanLynx software (version 4.1, Waters Corp., Milford, MA) and the analyte/internal standard peak area ratios were used for relative quantification. The mean analyte/internal standard peak area ratio for 16alpha-hydroxy DHEA-S was determined for the solvent control and was referred as the 100% control activity to calculate the percent remaining activity in samples containing increasing concentrations of PFOS. The GraphPad Prism software was used for dose-response curve fitting.
RESULTS:
PFAS Unique Binding Interactions with CYP3A7.

Of the six PFAS tested, PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, and PFHxS triggered unique changes in the heme Soret spectrum upon binding to the recombinant CYP3A7. These interactions featured two distinct binding events at similar wavelengths consistent across all four PFAS: reverse Type I binding (lambda 430 - 436 nm), and Type I binding (lambda 365 - 371 nm); each representative peak in the spectra share a trough (lambda 410 - 415 nm) as well (Figure 2) (Table 1). This spectral behavior demonstrated negative cooperativity with the reverse Type I binding initially observed during the titration, but then a shift occurred wherein Type I binding occurred as the enzyme became more saturated with each PFAS compound. This inverse relationship favors the first reverse Type I binding event which is demonstrated by lower Kd values for the initial interaction compared to that of the second Type I binding event.

PFOA [2.5 - 600 muM] demonstrated its initial reverse Type I binding event at lambda = 436 nm, Kd = 237.5 muM (R2= 0.975), and its second Type I binding event at lambda = 370 nm, Kd = 477.9 muM (R2= 0.990). The first binding event for PFOS [2.5 - 200 muM] occurred at lambda = 434 nm, Kd = 61.74 muM (R2= 0.970), and its second binding event occurred at lambda = 365 nm, Kd = 90.39 muM (R2= 0.973). PFNA [30 - 700 muM] exhibited its reverse Type I behavior at lambda = 435 nm, Kd = 76.87 muM (R2= 0.894), and its Type I binding at lambda = 371 nm, Kd = 181.2 muM (R2= 0.923). PFHxS [50 - 1500 muM] demonstrated its initial binding event at lambda = 430 nm, Kd = 296.8 muM (R2= 0.977), and its Type I binding at lambda = 365 nm, Kd = 731.3 muM (R2= 0.962) (Figure 2) (Table 1).

The PFAS compounds with carboxylic acid head groups (PFOA and PFNA) demonstrated binding peaks and troughs at proportionately higher wavelengths for both binding events compared to PFAS compounds with sulfonic acid head groups (PFOS and PFHxS) (Figure 2). In addition, longer chain length, and possession of a sulfonic acid head group appeared to result in more effective binding, as evidenced by the lower Kd values observed (Table 1). GenX and PFNS did not demonstrate any spectral interactions with rCYP3A7 in these experiments.
Positive controls for Type I (Lopinavir) and Type II (Ketoconazole) binding demonstrated respective Kd values of 6.482 muM (R2 = 0.992) and 23.24 muM (R2 = 0.997) (Table 1, Figure S1).
In-silico Docking Studies Provide Structural Support for the Type I and Reverse Type I PFAS-CYP3A7 Interactions.

PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, and PFHxS all demonstrated energetically favorable docking poses consistent with reverse Type I and Type I interactions with the CYP3A7 heme iron observed in our previous binding experiments (Figure 3). Reverse Type I interactions featured the closest distances (A), and lowest binding energies (kcal/mol) between the oxygen heteroatom of each PFAS compound and the heme iron: PFOA (Figure 3, panel A: 3.427 A; -7.7 kcal/mol), PFOS (Figure 3, panel C: 3.149 A; -7.9 kcal/mol), PFNA (Figure 3, panel E: 3.400 A; -8.2 kcal/mol) and PFHxS (Figure 3, panel G: 3.078 A; -7.2 kcal/mol) (q.f. Table 2). These configurations involved the PFAS of interest docking in a perpendicular fashion to the heme iron with the hydrophilic head groups oriented towards the heme and the alkyl chain tail pointing away from the center of the active site. Docking poses representative of a Type I interaction between the omega-1 carbon of each PFAS and the heme iron consisted of slightly longer distances between the PFAS molecule omega-1 carbon and the heme iron when compared to the distances retrieved from the PFAS oxygen hetero atom. In addition, the heme iron in the reverse Type I pose indicated higher binding energies compared to those of the Type I poses observed for all the PFAS compounds examined: PFOA (Figure 3, panel A: 4.346 A; -8.3 kcal/mol), PFOS (Figure 3, panel C: 5.818 A; -8.0 kcal/mol), PFNA (Figure 3, panel E: 4.054 A; -8.3 kcal/mol) and PFHxS (Figure 3, panel G: 4.279 A; -7.5 kcal/mol) (q.v. Table 2). Type I binding configurations involved each PFAS docking parallel to the heme iron with the omega-1 carbon oriented above the heme, and the hydrophilic head groups pointed in the opposite direction away from the heme iron.
PFAS Inhibition of CYP3A7 Oxidative Activity.

All four PFAS compounds that bound to CYP3A7 (PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, and PFHxS) also demonstrated inhibition of the enzyme in the DBF oxidation assay when tested at both 10 and 100 muM concentrations (Figure 4). PFOS was observed to be the most potent inhibitor at both concentrations tested, whereas PFOA was the least potent. Percent inhibition (+- SD) of CYP3A7 DBF oxidation at 10 muM PFOS was 35.1% +- 2.99 and 71.5% +- 1.66 at 100 muM PFOS. Inhibitory potency of PFOS was followed by PFNA at 23.9% +- 0.593 (10 muM PFNA) and 58.8% +- 3.15 (100 muM PFNA) along with PFHxS at 29.1% +- 4.19 (10 muM PFHxS) and 48.8% +- 1.63 (100 muM PFHxS). Our least potent inhibitor, PFOA, inhibited the reaction at 16.3% +- 0.275 (10 muM PFOA) and 35.8% +- 4.76 (100 muM PFOA) percent inhibition of CYP3A7 activity (Figure 4). This data was consistent with our findings from the PFAS binding studies with recombinant CYP3A7.
Quantitative Determination of the Extent of Inhibition of PFAS and PFNA CYP3A7 DBF Oxidation.

IC50 values were determined for two of the most potent inhibitors of CYP3A7 DBF oxidation, PFOS and PFNA (Figure 5). As the IC50 data illustrates, PFOS had the lowest half maximal inhibitory concentration with an IC50 value of 20.39 muM (R2 = 0.981) compared to that of PFNA, which had an IC50 of 137.6 muM (R2 = 0.978) (Figure 5, A-B). This data is consistent with that of our PFAS inhibition screening and binding studies.
Quantitative Determination of the Inhibition Extent of PFOS for CYP3A7 DHEA-S Hydroxylation.

The in vitro inhibitory potency of PFOS, the most potent PFAS for the CYP3A7 DBF oxidation, was then assessed for the CYP3A7 16alpha-hydroxylation of the adrenal steroid hormone DHEA-S (Figure 6). DHEA-S, at the Km concentration of 5 muM, was incubated with the CYP3A7 bactosomes and a concentration range of PFOS. An IC50 value of 16.75 muM (R2 = 0.980) was estimated which was consistent with that of the DBF oxidation assay (Figure 5).
DISCUSSION:

In recent years, the class of compounds collectively known as PFAS has garnered a significant amount of attention due to their widespread environmental contamination and the subsequent lingering health effects caused by human exposure to them. These include certain types of cancer, hepatotoxicity, and immune dysfunction, as well as birth and developmental defects. While clear associations between these compounds and their adverse effects on human health exist, the underlying molecular toxicological mechanisms have remained elusive. From a chemical perspective they bear a structural resemblance to fatty acids, although their preponderance of C-F bonds make them unlike any naturally occurring fatty acid-type molecules, while contributing to their unique physiochemical properties. Since the C-F bond does not occur in the biological context, it is reasonable to assume that it is unlikely that these compounds would undergo significant metabolism by fatty acid hydroxylases or CYP enzymes. However, their ultra-hydrophobic nature would suggest that they may be effective competitive inhibitors of these enzymes, given the hydrophobicity of CYP active sites. Since CYP enzymes are involved in a significant number of critical biological processes, including regulation of the immune system (through arachidonic acid oxidation), development of cancer, and fetal growth and development, this inhibition could have profound implications for the human pathologies observed with these compounds.

Based on our findings presented in this study, it is clear that PFAS compounds can bind to (Figures 2,3) and inhibit (Figures 4,5) CYP3A7 function in vitro. The unique nature of the absorption difference spectra demonstrates two distinct binding events between recombinant CYP3A7 and four of six PFAS tested (PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, and PFHxS) (Figure 2). This behavior is indicative of a negatively cooperative relationship which arises from the lower Kd values obtained for the second binding event across all four PFAS compounds when compared to those of the first binding event. Interestingly, negative cooperativity in ligand binding has been reported previously for CYP3A enzymes. In Roberts et al., it was observed that testosterone binds to CYP3A4 exhibiting negative cooperativity. The authors concluded that an initial high-affinity testosterone binding event was followed by the binding of a second testosterone molecule with a lower-affinity, hence demonstrating negative cooperativity for this closely related enzyme.

Due to the spectral characteristics of the absorption difference spectra obtained from our ligand binding studies, we can deduce that the first binding event in each case is representative of reverse Type I binding, in which a negatively charged oxygen atom from the PFAS head group displaces the axial water ligand to form a coordinate covalent bond with the heme iron in the binding pocket of the CYP or, alternatively, the ligand forms a bond with the heme iron via a bridged water atom, as observed with certain substrates and inhibitors. This interaction occurs at a lower Kd and PFAS concentration compared to the second binding event, indicating a higher affinity for this particular binding pose. As the PFAS concentration increases throughout the titration, the binding behavior switches to the more energetically favorable Type I binding mode, indicated by a separate peak arriving in our absorbance spectra at ~375 nm. As the initial reverse Type I complex becomes saturated, the PFAS binds in a parallel orientation to the heme, likely to avoid electrostatic repulsion between the negative heteroatoms in the ligand head groups. This, in turn, displaces the first molecule from coordination with the heme, resulting in a Type I spectrum.

Our docking simulations reinforce this interpretation of the data. As can be seen in Figure 3, panel A, one of the most energetically favorable poses for PFOA shows it in a perpendicular orientation in regard to the position of the carboxylic acid and the heme iron, with a distance of 3.247 A between the alcohol oxygen and the heme iron, indicative of a reverse Type I interaction (distances of less than 5 A are generally considered significant for an interaction). Another favorable binding pose indicated that PFOA could also bind in a horizontal orientation with respect to the heme (Figure 3, panel B), in this case with the hydrophobic end of the molecule within 4.346 A of the heme iron. Similar docking poses were also obtained with PFOS, PFNA, and PFHxS (Figure 3, panels C-H, respectively), indicating a consistent mode of interaction between the different PFAS compounds and CYP3A7.

The significant differences in the Bmax values point to the fact that the individual respective ligands have differential effects on the spin-state conversion of the heme iron (Figure 2). It has been noted previously that certain ligands may be more effective in promoting spin-state conversion of the heme iron to the high (or low) spin-state forms (Hlavica, P., 2007). In the case of the PFAS compounds, surprisingly the trend is that the weaker binding compounds (PFOA and PFHxS) produced the greatest Bmax, indicating spin-state conversion for an increased portion of the enzyme (Figure 2). The only exception to this was the second binding event detected for PFNA, which produced the largest Bmax (the Bmax for the initial binding events for PFNA and PFHxS were similar). While PFOS has a lower half maximal inhibitory concentration than PFNA, the inhibition by PFOS is only decreased to ~30% activity of the control reaction, whereas PFNA reaches total inhibition (Figure 4). This could be related to observed difference in Bmax values, as noted above (Figure 2).

The Kd values from our binding studies were consistent with our results from both the CYP3A7 inhibition and IC50 experiments. Of the PFAS tested, PFOS displayed the highest affinity for CYP3A7 through its interaction with the heme iron. In addition, PFOS was our most potent inhibitor of CYP3A7 oxidative activity, in which 10 muM [PFOS] resulted in 35.1% inhibition, and 100 muM [PFOS] achieved 71.5% inhibition. This potency is likely due to the presence of the sulfate group in the hydrophilic portion of the alkyl chain, which is an important binding moiety in the endogenous ligand of CYP3A7, DHEA-S. In contrast, the increased carbon chain length in PFNA resulted in a lower affinity than PFOA and similarly, a lower inhibition potency, allowing it to reach 23.9% inhibition at 10 muM [PFNA] and 58.8% inhibition at 100 muM [PFNA] (Figure 4). Given that PFNA has a lower affinity for rCYP3A7 compared to PFOS, and that PFNS did not bind to rCYP3A7, it is clear that alkyl chain length is not solely determinative of PFAS inhibitory potential of the enzyme. In terms of these interactions, it appears that PFAS compounds containing a sulfonic acid head group do not benefit from a chain length beyond 8-carbons, whereas compounds possessing a carboxylic head group can compensate for their weaker affinity for the heme iron through a longer alkyl chain that facilitates hydrophobic interactions. Further research is needed to understand how this unique paradox operates on a biochemical level.

The initial observations we made of the Kd values in our spectral binding studies indicated low-affinity interactions between PFAS and the heme iron in the binding pocket of CYP3A7 compared to other ligands. For example, lopinavir and ketoconazole bound to CYP3A7 with Kd values of 6.482 muM (R2 = 0.992) and 23.24 muM (R2 = 0.997), respectively (Table 1, Figure S1). Lopinavir possesses a terminal elimination half-life of 2.33 to 2.44 hours depending on dosage frequency [Boffito et al., 2008, International Medical Press]. Ketoconazole has a biphasic half-life of about two hours for the first 10 hours following a dose, and then a terminal half-life of about 8 years. Although serum PFAS concentrations present in the nanomolar range, PFAS half-lives can reach 5 years in human tissues. In addition, both lopinavir and ketoconazole are active substrates of CYP enzymes, namely CYP3A4, and their mechanisms of clearance are well-established in the literature. It has not been established whether PFAS compounds can be metabolized in humans. The compounds are thought to be eliminated in the bile and urine, and are known to undergo enterohepatic recirculation, as well as become reabsorbed in renal tubules, allowing for increased biological permanence compared to other CYP3A7 inhibitors. Thus, given their long half-lives and propensity to accumulate in the liver, the PFAS compounds examined here may be effective competitive inhibitors of endogenous CYP3A7 ligands, such as DHEA-S and atRA.

Indeed, PFOS showed significant inhibition potency for CYP3A7 in vitro 16alpha-hydroxylation of DHEA-S with an IC50 of 16.8 muM, in particular when considering that the Km for DHEA-S is approximately 5 muM. Further research is needed to determine whether the PFAS compounds studied here have an impact on CYP3A7 oxidation of DHEA-S and atRA in vivo. Furthermore, testing PFAS interactions with other CYP enzymes involved in development would provide additional insight into the specific biochemical implications of exposure.

Overall, our data demonstrate unique inhibitory interactions between prominent PFAS, and the important fetal cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP3A7. Future efforts may shed light on specific in vivo biochemical mechanisms of toxicity of this important class of environmental pollutants.
